chunks.source: FEDERAL RULES OF CIVIL PROCEDURE / Rules Suggestions
chunks.title: 26-cv-17 suggestion from ford toyota volkswagen hyundai - rule 23 (3)
chunks.content:
amendment will equip judges with a practical tool to manage their dockets and promote true
judicial efficiency. The Problem: The “Adjudication” Blindfold
The foundational mandate of the Federal Rules is to secure the “just, speedy, and
inexpensive” determination of every action. Fed. R. Civ. P. 1. The current application of Rule
23(b)(3) undermines all three of these goals by placing a blindfold on the judiciary. When an automaker identifies a potential issue, it routinely implements non-judicial
remedies, such as recalls, service actions, customer satisfaction programs, or direct customer
interventions. These measures identify owners, notify them, and provide free repairs or
reimbursements where appropriate. Whether overseen by federal regulators or initiated
proactively by the manufacturer, these programs provide an immediate, direct cure. Class action
litigation, by contrast, often results in delayed, piecemeal payments diluted by significant
administrative costs and attorney fees. The current interpretation of Rule 23(b)(3) forces courts to ignore this reality. Because
the Rule asks if a class action is superior to other “methods for . . . adjudicating the controversy,”
many courts interpret this text to exclude non-judicial remedies.

They feel compelled to
compare the class action only to other lawsuits, blinding themselves to the swifter, more
complete remedy of a recall, customer satisfaction program, or individual customer intervention,
solely because it is not an “adjudication.” While these non-judicial solutions and a narrowly
defined “adjudication” differ, the former are often superior: they provide direct, fast, and fair
relief to consumers without draining judicial resources. These characteristics align far better
with Rule 1. This narrow reading of “adjudication” forces judges to disregard these benefits, creating a
disconnect between practical efficiency and judicial outcomes. For example, in In re Hannaford
Bros. Co. Consumer Data Sec. Breach Litig., the court noted that a defendant’s refund program
was likely better for consumers than litigation. Yet the court felt compelled to ignore it because
Rule 23(b)(3) “does not address superiority as a matter of abstract economic choice analysis,”
but strictly as a comparison of “adjudication” methods. 293 F.R.D. 21, 34-35 (D. Me. 2013). The proposed amendment resolves this disconnect, empowering judges to credit practical
remedies rather than defaulting to the protracted waste of the “car parts” docket. Restoring this discretion to evaluate non-judicial remedies is not a leap into the unknown.

chunks.source: FEDERAL RULES OF CIVIL PROCEDURE / Rules Suggestions
chunks.title: 26-cv-17 suggestion from ford toyota volkswagen hyundai - rule 23 (5)
chunks.content:
Before the 2011 Aqua Dots decision, courts frequently applied a common-sense approach,
recognizing that a class action was not “superior” if the defendant or regulator was already
providing relief. See, e.g., Berley v. Dreyfus & Co., 43 F.R.D. 397 (S.D.N.Y. 1967) (denying
certification where a refund was already offered); Kamm v. Cal. City Dev. Co., 509 F.2d 205 (9th
Cir. 1975) (finding a state administrative action superior to a class action); Chin v. Chrysler
Corp., 182 F.R.D. 448, 463 (D.N.J. 1998) (finding a voluntary automotive recall superior to a
class action). Harmonizing Rule 23 with Judicial Economy
Rules Suggestion 26-CV-17

-- 2 of 4 --

chunks.source: FEDERAL RULES OF CIVIL PROCEDURE / Rules Suggestions
chunks.title: 26-cv-17 suggestion from ford toyota volkswagen hyundai - rule 23 (6)
chunks.content:
Our proposal would harmonize Rule 23 with established doctrines of judicial restraint
and economy, such as primary jurisdiction and prudential mootness. This approach also aligns
with the foundational principle that class actions are a procedural exception, not the default. Federal courts already recognize that when a “coordinate branch of government”
oversees a remedy, the judiciary should step back to avoid “needless duplication and inter-branch
disputes.” Winzler v. Toyota Motor Sales U.S.A., Inc., 681 F.3d 1208, 1210-12 (10th Cir. 2012). In those cases, courts dismiss the action as prudentially moot because the regulator (e.g., the
National Highway Traffic Safety Administration) and automaker are resolving the problem. The amendment we propose would codify similar logic in the Rule 23 superiority
analysis. It would give judges the express authority to say: “Because the defendant is already
providing full relief through a non-judicial remedial program, a class action is not superior.”
This empowers district courts to apply the logic of mootness—avoiding redundancy— to clear
their dockets of resolved disputes, without being shackled by a rule that currently lurches
towards certification even when the remedy was provided years prior. Crucially, avoiding this redundancy does not close the courthouse doors to individual
litigants.

chunks.source: FEDERAL RULES OF CIVIL PROCEDURE / Rules Suggestions
chunks.title: 26-cv-17 suggestion from ford toyota volkswagen hyundai - rule 23 (7)
chunks.content:
If a consumer believes they suffered unique damages not covered by the automaker’s
program, they remain free to pursue an individual action. The proposed amendment addresses
only the class mechanism, a procedural exception, not the default mode of dispute resolution. Its
purpose is to aggregate claims only when it is the most efficient method of adjudication. If a
defendant has already established a program to make the class whole, the class action device
loses its utility. Arguments that class litigation is necessary to uncover the “truth” through discovery ring
hollow when a comprehensive remedy is already being implemented. Forcing parties to engage
in years of costly discovery to litigate a problem that a manufacturer already resolved directly
with its customers, oftentimes with federal regulator oversight, serves no truth-seeking function
and merely clogs federal dockets. Addressing Downstream Effects: This Is Not a “Free Pass”
We wish to be clear: This amendment does not create a safe harbor for sham non-judicial
remedies. This is because the proposed change does not mandate a denial of certification
whenever a recall or customer satisfaction program exists. If a defendant offers a “sham”
remedy, imposes high barriers to entry, or provides less than a full cure, the judge retains full
authority to find the class action vehicle is superior.

chunks.source: FEDERAL RULES OF CIVIL PROCEDURE / Rules Suggestions
chunks.title: 26-cv-17 suggestion from ford toyota volkswagen hyundai - rule 23 (8)
chunks.content:
As such, fears that this amendment would
allow defendants to “grade their own papers” are unfounded. The amendment instead enhances
the integrity of Rule 23 by empowering judges to evaluate the full remedial picture, ensuring the
class device is used only when truly necessary. Rules Suggestion 26-CV-17

-- 3 of 4 --

Conclusion
Federal courts exist to resolve genuine disputes that cannot be resolved elsewhere. When
a defendant provides the remedy that plaintiffs seek outside the litigation, the dispute is over.
We are not asking for a rule that forces a specific outcome, but rather a tool that allows judges to
weigh all available information when managing their cases. We therefore urge the Committee to
adopt the LCJ suggestion and remove the textual blinders that force courts to ignore superior,
non-judicial solutions.
Sincerely,

The seminal study on social security numbers was published in 2009 by Carnegie Mellon
professors Alessandro Acquisti and Ralph Gross, who found that social security numbers have the
same safety level as a three-digit pin.6 This research determined that with the right methods, SSNs

tax lien records, property records, death certificates, and even missing persons

increased the ease with which one can learn a potential victim’s SSN.9

III. Privacy Is Collective Responsibility. It is incumbent upon all of us—individuals, employers, the government, and the court—to protect
privacy. Hackers, bad actors, and cyber threats are everywhere. The absence of an obvious case or
archetypal rules issue does not absolve the rules committees from their role in the collective
responsibility to modernize the judiciary’s privacy practices. This obligation to take proactive
measures is especially critical since it would be extremely difficult to bring an individual claim
showing that one’s identity was stolen, hacked, or otherwise compromised by the required
disclosures in a court filing. In the first place, if one is already a named party in a case, the resolution
of the case is likely a higher priority. Secondly, privacy claims associated with fraud and identity theft
will require a class action to address the cause of harm.18 Failure to address an issue until there is
evidence of a problem does not align with the values of fairness and justice. IV. AAJ Urges Full Redaction of SSNs. Americans must worry about their private information being hacked from their personal phones and
computers, the businesses where they bank and shop, their employers, and even the government. The courts should help parties by not contributing to the risk of identity theft and other privacy
violations.

with documents being only available at courthouses.)
Civil Rule 5.2(c)
As a general matter, remote PACER access to civil immigration case documents is
barred by Fed. R. Civ. P. 5.2(c), which seeks to strike a balance the privacy interest of
litigants against the public interest, and is written with the presumption that there is
generally not a lot of public interest in such cases. The public is required to go to the
courthouse during clerk’s office business hours to view or obtain a filing. With the increased prevalence of “impact” immigration litigation over the past decade,
that balance becomes more questionable.

That compromise has had the effect of reducing the volume of motion practice to

Effective Feb. 1, 1977, as amended to Dec. 1, 2019
Rule 1. Scope
(a) Cases Involving a Petition under 28 U.S.C. § 2254. These rules govern a petition for a writ of habeas corpus filed in a
United States district court under 28 U.S.C. § 2254 by:
(1) a person in custody under a state-court judgment
who seeks a determination that the custody violates the Constitution, laws, or treaties of the United States; and
(2) a person in custody under a state-court or federalcourt judgment who seeks a determination that future custody under a state-court judgment would violate the Constitution, laws, or
treaties of the United States. (b) Other Cases. The district court may apply any or all of
these rules to a habeas corpus petition not covered by Rule 1(a). Rule 2. The Petition
(a) Current Custody; Naming the Respondent. If the petitioner is currently in custody under a state-court judgment, the petition must name as respondent the state officer who has custody. (b) Future Custody; Naming the Respondents and Specifying the Judgment. If the petitioner is not yet in custody - but
may be subject to future custody - under the state-court judgment
being contested, the petition must name as respondents both the
officer who has current custody and the attorney general of the
state where the judgment was entered.

Effective Feb. 1, 1977, as amended to Dec. 1, 2019
Rule 1. Scope
These rules govern a motion filed in a United States district court
under 28 U.S.C. § 2255 by:
(a) a person in custody under a judgment of that court who
seeks a determination that:
(1) the judgment violates the Constitution or laws of the
United States;
(2) the court lacked jurisdiction to enter the judgment;
(3) the sentence exceeded the maximum allowed by law;
or
(4) the judgment or sentence is otherwise subject to collateral review; and
(b) a person in custody under a judgment of a state court or
another federal court, and subject to future custody under a judgment of the district court, who seeks a determination that:
(1) future custody under a judgment of the district court
would violate the Constitution or laws of the United States;
(2) the district court lacked jurisdiction to enter the judgment;
(3) the district court's sentence exceeded the maximum
allowed by law; or

subject to collateral review.

awning into street, after construction and acceptance. Oklahoma City R. Co. v. Boyd, (1929) 140 Okla. 45, 282 P. 157. Flooding from embankment, after construction and acceptance. Walker v. Strosnider, (1910) 67 W. Va. 39, 67 S.E. 1089. Impairment of lateral support of adjoining land, while construction in progress. S.H. Kress & Co. v. Reaves, (4 Cir. 1936) 85 F. 2d 915. The same. On the other hand there appears to be a definite distinction, as
to either construction or repair, between the situation where the premises are turned over to the contractor and he is in possession and
full control of them during the progress of the work, and that where
the employer remains in possession and retains some control over the
premises during the work, or has resumed it after completion. Where
the contractor is in full control most of the cases--except as to
lateral support, which appears to be a special case (see § 422A)hold that the employer is not liable for the contractor's negligence,
unless the case can be brought within same other exception, such as

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
Where the work is construction, it is normal for the premises to be turned over entirely to the
contractor. It is unusual in cases of repair. This appears to be the
true distinction, which the Council were groping for in 1930 when they
inserted the Caveat. See the following cases:
Boswell v. Laird, (1857) 8 Cal. 469. Injury caused when an embankment and dam were washed out by a flood. The construction work was in
progress, and the land in the hands of the contractor. No liability. Prest-o-Lite Co. v. Skeel, (1914) 182 Ind. 593, 106 N.E. 365. Injury to a workman while work in progress on premises turned over to
the contractor. No liability of the employer. Burke v. Ireland, (1901) 166 N.Y. 305, 59 N.E. 914. Injury to a
workman employed by a subcontractor, while work was in progress on
premises turned over to the contractor. No liability of the employer. Besner v. Central Trust Co. of New York, (1921) 230 N.Y. 357, 130
N.E. 357. Injury to workman using elevator, caused by defective safety
doors of elevator in process of construction. Employer in possession;
held liable on the basis that it had permitted the use of the elevator
during the work.

Ch. 15

31
Gilmore v. Philadelphia & R. R. Co., (1893) 154 Pa. 375, 25 A. 774. Repair of a bridge, used as an approach to the railroad station. Injury
to an invitee. Employer held liable on the ground that it had permitted
use by its patrons before completion of the work. Lineaweaver v. John Wanamaker Philadelphia, (1930) 299 Pa. 45, 149
A. 91. Injury to a customer in a store through the fall of a monitor
above a skylight, during construction. Basis of the liability, that
defendant employer had permitted use of the store during the work. McCrorey v. Thomas, (1909) 109 Va. 373, 63 S.E. 1011. Fall of an
awning from a building into the street, during construction. The court
said that the employer would be liable if it had occurred after completion of the work and acceptance, but not if it occurred while the work
was in progress in the hands of the contractor. Reporter Bohlen saw this distinction (Explanatory Notes, p. 42),
but did not stress it. Apparently it got lost somewhere along the way
through his Advisers and the Council. It accounts for two large groups
of cases which simply do not fit into the old Section as stated. One
of these agrees in holding that the employer is not liable, except possibly on the basis of "inherent danger" (see § 427) for the negligence
of the contractor in doing demolition work-tearing down buildings
taking down walls, etc.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
See the cases collected in 32 A.L.R. 2d 92 ff. There is no possible way to distinguish such work in principle from
construction or repair. If anything, the danger is greater. The
explanation must lie in the fact that for demolition work the premises
are invariably turned over to the contractor entirely, and the employer
relinquishes all possession and control. The other group of cases hold,
in considerable number, that the employer is not liable to employees of
the contractor, or of subcontractors. See cases collected in 44 A.L.R. 932 ff. Again it is not easy to distinguish on any basis of theory,
since such employees are business visitors of the employer if he remains in possession. Again, as an examination of the cases indicates,
the explanation appears to lie in the fact that in the cases denying
liability the premises, or the part of them on which the work was done,
were turned over to the contractor, and he was in full control. The Section has been changed accordingly. The Advisers, and the
Council, all agree.

transportation on water. (July 30, 1947, ch. 388, 61 Stat. 633.)
§ 4. ‘‘Vehicle’’ as including all means of land
transportation
The word ‘‘vehicle’’ includes every description
of carriage or other artificial contrivance used,
or capable of being used, as a means of transportation on land. (July 30, 1947, ch. 388, 61 Stat. 633.)

Enrolled bills and resolutions of either House
of Congress shall be printed on parchment or
paper of suitable quality as shall be determined

§ 108. Repeal of repealing act
Whenever an Act is repealed, which repealed a
former Act, such former Act shall not thereby
be revived, unless it shall be expressly so provided. (July 30, 1947, ch. 388, 61 Stat. 635.)
§ 109. Repeal of statutes as affecting existing liabilities
The repeal of any statute shall not have the
effect to release or extinguish any penalty, forfeiture, or liability incurred under such statute,
unless the repealing Act shall so expressly provide, and such statute shall be treated as still
remaining in force for the purpose of sustaining
any proper action or prosecution for the enforcement of such penalty, forfeiture, or liability. The expiration of a temporary statute shall not
have the effect to release or extinguish any penalty, forfeiture, or liability incurred under such
statute, unless the temporary statute shall so
expressly provide, and such statute shall be
treated as still remaining in force for the purpose of sustaining any proper action or prosecution for the enforcement of such penalty, forfeiture, or liability. (July 30, 1947, ch. 388, 61 Stat. 635.)

§ 422
32
Torts
Comment:
a. Persons travelling on a highway or persons
rightfully on private land seldom know or have the
means of ascertaining the arrangements which a possessor of adjacent lands makes for the maintenance of
the buildings and structures thereon. The possessor
of the adjacent land owes a duty to them to maintain
it in a reasonably safe condition (see §§ 364 to 370). They are therefore entitled to look to him for protection, and he is required to answer for the negligent
manner in which repairs are made upon the buildings
and structures by an independent contractor whom he
employs to do all or any part of the work of making
the repairs or ascertaining the need thereof
duty which a possessor of land owes to others to put
and maintain in reasonably safe condition is nondelegable. If an independent eontractor, no matter
how carefully selected, is employed to perform it, the
possessor is answerable for harm caused by the negligent failure of his contractor to put or maintain the
buildings and structures in reasonably safe condition,
irrespective of whether the contractor's negligence lies
in his incompetence, carelessness, inattention or delay. The
The rule stated in this Section applies in favor of any
person toward whom the possessor of land is under a duty with respect
to the physical condition of the land.

other structure on the land, whether it be construction, repair or
demolition. It applies to work done on the land itself preparatory

while the possessor has retained possession of the premises during
the progress of the work, or after he has resumed possession of the

turned over to the contractor, and he is in exclusive possession of
it. Thus where the employer moves out of his building and surren

of the land, possession of which has been turned over to the contractor. Possession usually is surrendered fully to the contractor in the case
of construction or demolition work, and it may be so surrendered in
cases of extensive repairs. Normally, however, the employer remains
in possession during ordinary repairs, and for that reason the rule
here stated is more frequently applied in such cases. Illustrations:
1. A, the owner of a department store, employs an independent

in progress, the monitor is insecurely fastened, and falls through
the skylight, injuring B, a customer in the aisle of the store. A is subject to liability to B. 2. A, the owner of land, employs an independent contractor
to construct a building on the land. The premises are turned over
to the contractor, who enters into full possession and control of
them.

chunks.title: USCODE-2024-title11 (20)
chunks.content:
Courts should readily allow the rejection of such contracts where they are burdensome, the
rejection will aid in the municipality’s reorganization
and in consideration of the equities of each case. On the
last point, ‘‘[e]quities in favor of the city in chapter 9
will be far more compelling than the equities in favor
of the employer in chapter 11. Onerous employment obligations may prevent a city from balancing its budget
for some time. The prospect of an unbalanced budget
may preclude judicial confirmation of the plan. Unless
a city can reject its labor contracts, lack of funds may
force cutbacks in police, fire, sanitation, and welfare
services, imposing hardships on many citizens. In addition, because cities in the past have often seemed immune to the constraint of ‘‘profitability’’ faced by private businesses, their wage contracts may be relatively
more onerous than those in the private sector.’’ Executory Contracts and Municipal Bankruptcy, 85 Yale L. J. 957, 965 (1976) (footnote omitted). Rejection of the contracts may require the municipalities to renegotiate
such contracts by state collective bargaining laws. It is
intended that the power to reject collective bargaining
agreements will pre-empt state termination provisions,
but not state collective bargaining laws. Thus, a city
would not be required to maintain existing employment terms during the renegotiation period.

VALIDITY OF DISABLING RESTRAINTS
Disabling restraints in donative transfers,
other than those imposed on equitable interests under
a trust, are invalid.
Comment:
a.
Rationale.
All restraints on alienation
run counter to the policy of freedom of alienation
so that to be upheld they must in some way be
justified. But disabling restraints have an additional objection to their validity since to be effective they must enable the person restrained to deny
the validity of such person's own transfer and
also, unless the restraint is only as to voluntary
transfers, to deny such person's creditors resort
to the property interests which such person is
enjoying. The result is the rule stated in this

In any event, this new section merely confirms past
and present practice, and restores, if it does not preserve, statutory authority for possession and use of the
seal which is a very necessary part of the operations of
the Bureau. Further, the section should serve to forestall future differences of interpretation. In the past,
some States have refused to recognize the seal of the
Census Bureau on the ground that it was not authorized by law. In all probability, this position was taken,
not as the result of a search of the Statutes at Large,
which would have been a difficult project, but because
provisions relating to the seal were not set out in the
United States Code where they would have been readily
accessible. The language of this section follows substantially the
language of section 31 of the act of Mar. 3, 1899, referred
to above, but has been reworded because of jurisdictional and other changes since that time. The ‘‘Census
Office’’ was transferred from the Department of the Interior to the Department of Commerce and Labor by

1913, ch. 141, § 1, 37 Stat. 736, changed the name of the
latter to the Department of Commerce, and created, as
a separate department, the Department of Labor.

(13
U.S.C. 141(a).)
Once the Secretary, through the Director of the U.S. Census Bureau, takes the count, the President must
carry out the apportionment of Representatives among
the States. The Secretary prepares the ‘‘tabulation of
total population by States . . . as required for the apportionment of Representatives,’’ and reports that tabulation to the President. (13 U.S.C. 141(b).) The President then sends a statement to the Congress showing
‘‘the whole number of persons in each State,’’ as
ascertained under the census, and ‘‘the number of Representatives to which each State would be entitled
under’’ the equal proportions apportionment method. (2
U.S.C. 2a(a).) The Clerk of the House of Representatives
then transmits to each State a certification of the
number of seats that the State receives under that apportionment. (2 U.S.C. 2a(b).) Finally, within 1 year of
the decennial census date, the Secretary must also report to the Governor and officers or public bodies having responsibility for legislative apportionment or districting of each State the population tabulations to be
used for apportioning districts within that State. (13
U.S.C. 141(c).)
At no point since our Nation’s Founding has a person’s immigration status alone served as a basis for excluding that person from the total population count
used in apportionment.

Ch. 15
§ 422A
37
$422A. WORK WITHDRAWING LATERAL SUPPORT
ONE WHO EMPLOYS AN INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR TO DO WORK WHICH THE
EMPLOYER KNOWS OR SHOULD KNOW TO BE LIKELY TO WITHDRAW LATERAL SUPPORT
FROM THE LAND OF ANOTHER IS SUBJECT TO THE SAME LIABILITY FOR THE
CONTRACTOR'S WITHDRAWAL OF SUCH SUPPORT AS IF THE EMPLOYER HAD
RETAINED THE WORK IN HIS OWN HANDS. Comment:
a. Under the rule stated in § 817, one who withdraws the naturally
necessary lateral support of the land of another, or support which has
been substituted for the naturally necessary support, is liable for a
subsidence of the land, even though he is in no way negligent in doing
An exception to this is stated in § 818, as to subsidence resulting from the withdrawal of subterranean water. Under the rule stated
in 819, one who withdraws lateral support for artificial additions to
the land of another is subject to liability if he is negligent in doing
So. b. Under the rule stated in this Section, one who employs an independent contractor to do work involving excavation, or other work of a
kind which the employer knows or should know to be likely to result in
the withdrawal of lateral support from the land of another, is subject
to the same liability for a withdrawal of such support by the contractor
as if he had retained the work in his own hands.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
Thus if naturally necessary support is withdrawn, the employer is subject to liability even if
the contractor is not negligent in withdrawing it, except as to subterranean waters. On the other hand, if support necessary only for artificial additions to the land is withdrawn, the employer is subject to liability for the negligence of the contractor, but is not liable if the
contractor has not been negligent.

EXCEPT AS STATED IN §§ 428 AND 429, AN EMPLOYER OF AN INDEPENDENT

to describe the kind of negligence referred to in this Section is "collateral negligence." For that reason alone it should appear in the title,
and "collateral" has to be explained in the Comments. Since this Section was drawn in 1931, the whole approach of the
courts and of legal writers to this problem has been very much affected
by a noted article by Talbot Smith, Collateral Negligence, (1941) 25

‘‘(a) FINDINGS.—Congress finds that—
‘‘(1) Craig Thomas was raised on a ranch just outside of Cody, Wyoming, near Yellowstone National
Park and Grand Teton National Park, where he—
‘‘(A) began a lifelong association with those
parks; and
‘‘(B) developed a deep and abiding dedication to

service in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, Craig Thomas forged a distinguished
legislative record on issues as diverse as public land

strong proponent for ensuring that people of all ages
and abilities had a wide range of opportunities to
learn more about the natural and cultural heritage of
the United States;

critical funding and management reforms to protect
units of the National Park System into the 21st century, ensuring quality visits to units of the National
Park System and the protection of natural and cultural resources;
‘‘(5) Craig Thomas strongly supported public-private partnerships and collaboration between the National Park Service and other organizations that foster new opportunities for providing visitor services
while encouraging greater citizen involvement in the
stewardship of units of the National Park System;
‘‘(6) Craig Thomas was instrumental in obtaining
the Federal share for a public-private partnership
with the Grand Teton National Park Foundation and
the Grand Teton Natural History Association to construct a new discovery and visitor center at Grand

after battling cancer for 7 months;

and children, Patrick, Greg, Peter, and Lexie; and

role of Craig Thomas in the new discovery and visitor

and he negligently handles his paint bucket in such a way that it goes

mortar from the wall over plaintiff's adjoining windows and the clothes
hanging in her yard. The employer is liable. Pye v. Faxon, (1892) 156
Mass. 471, 31 N.E. 640. But if the contractor splashes mortar from a
mortar box on the ground into the eye of a man passing by on the sidewalk, it is "collateral negligence," and the employer is not liable. Strauss v. City of Louisville, (1900) 108 Ky. 155, 55 S.W. 1075. 3. A contractor constructing a bridge over a public highway drops
a stone from the bridge, which injures a pedestrian below. The employer
is liable. Philadelphia, B. & W. R. Co. v. Mitchell, (1908) 107 Md. 600,

chunks.title: USCODE-2024-title17
chunks.content:
The test of separability and
independence from ‘‘the utilitarian aspects of the article’’ does not depend upon the nature of the design—
that is, even if the appearance of an article is determined by aesthetic (as opposed to functional) considerations, only elements, if any, which can be identified
separately from the useful article as such are copyrightable. And, even if the three-dimensional design
contains some such element (for example, a carving on
the back of a chair or a floral relief design on silver
flatware), copyright protection would extend only to
that element, and would not cover the over-all configuration of the utilitarian article as such. A special situation is presented by architectural
works. An architect’s plans and drawings would, of
course, be protected by copyright, but the extent to
which that protection would extend to the structure
depicted would depend on the circumstances. Purely
nonfunctional or monumental structures would be subject to full copyright protection under the bill, and the
same would be true of artistic sculpture or decorative
ornamentation or embellishment added to a structure. On the other hand, where the only elements of shape in
an architectural design are conceptually inseparable
from the utilitarian aspects of the structure, copyright
protection for the design would not be available.

The problem of off-the-air taping for nonprofit classroom use of copyrighted audiovisual works incorporated in radio and television broadcasts has proved
to be difficult to resolve. The Committee believes that
the fair use doctrine has some limited application in
this area, but it appears that the development of detailed guidelines will require a more thorough exploration than has so far been possible of the needs and
problems of a number of different interests affected,
and of the various legal problems presented. Nothing in
section 107 or elsewhere in the bill is intended to
change or prejudge the law on the point. On the other
hand, the Committee is sensitive to the importance of
the problem, and urges the representatives of the various interests, if possible under the leadership of the
Register of Copyrights, to continue their discussions
actively and in a constructive spirit. If it would be
helpful to a solution, the Committee is receptive to undertaking further consideration of the problem in a future Congress. The Committee appreciates and commends the efforts
and the cooperative and reasonable spirit of the parties
who achieved the agreed guidelines on books and periodicals and on music.

chunks.title: USCODE-2024-title17 (17)
chunks.content:
Without this change, the possibility of future United
States adherence to the Berne Copyright Union would
evaporate, but with it would come a great and immediate improvement in our copyright relations. All of
these benefits would accrue directly to American and
foreign authors alike. The need for a longer total term of copyright has
been conclusively demonstrated. It is true that a major
reason for the striking statistical increase in life expectancy since 1909 is the reduction in infant mortality, but this does not mean that the increase can be
discounted. Although not nearly as great as the total
increase in life expectancy, there has been a marked increase in longevity, and with medical discoveries and
health programs for the elderly this trend shows every
indication of continuing. If life expectancy in 1909,
which was in the neighborhood of 56 years, offered a
rough guide to the length of copyright protection, then
life expectancy in the 1970’s which is well over 70 years,
should offer a similar guide; the Register’s 1961 Report
included statistics indicating that something between
70 and 76 years was then the average equivalent of lifeplus-50 years. A copyright should extend beyond the author’s lifetime, and judged by this standard the present
term of 56 years is too short.

The principle of the divisibility of copyright ownership, established by section 201(d), carries with it the
need in infringement actions to safeguard the rights of
all copyright owners and to avoid a multiplicity of
suits. Subsection (b) of section 501 enables the owner of
a particular right to bring an infringement action in
that owner’s name alone, while at the same time insuring to the extent possible that the other owners whose
rights may be affected are notified and given a chance
to join the action. The first sentence of subsection (b) empowers the
‘‘legal or beneficial owner of an exclusive right’’ to

right committed while he or she is the owner of it.’’ A

§ 892. Making extortionate extensions of credit
(a) Whoever makes any extortionate extension
of credit, or conspires to do so, shall be fined
under this title or imprisoned not more than 20
years, or both. (b) In any prosecution under this section, if it
is shown that all of the following factors were
present in connection with the extension of
credit in question, there is prima facie evidence
that the extension of credit was extortionate,
but this subsection is nonexclusive and in no
way limits the effect or applicability of subsection (a):
(1) The repayment of the extension of credit,
or the performance of any promise given in
consideration thereof, would be unenforceable,
through civil judicial processes against the
debtor
(A) in the jurisdiction within which the
debtor, if a natural person, resided or
(B) in every jurisdiction within which the
debtor, if other than a natural person, was
incorporated or qualified to do business
at the time the extension of credit was made. (2) The extension of credit was made at a
rate of interest in excess of an annual rate of
45 per centum calculated according to the actuarial method of allocating payments made
on a debt between principal and interest, pursuant to which a payment is applied first to
the accumulated interest and the balance is
applied to the unpaid principal.

chunks.title: USCODE-2024-title18 (7)
chunks.content:
Licensing
(a) No person shall engage in the business of
importing, manufacturing, or dealing in firearms, or importing or manufacturing ammunition, until he has filed an application with and
received a license to do so from the Attorney
General. The application shall be in such form
and contain only that information necessary to
determine eligibility for licensing as the Attorney General shall by regulation prescribe and
shall include a photograph and fingerprints of
the applicant. Each applicant shall pay a fee for
obtaining such a license, a separate fee being required for each place in which the applicant is
to do business, as follows:
(1) If the applicant is a manufacturer—
(A) of destructive devices, ammunition for
destructive devices or armor piercing ammunition, a fee of $1,000 per year;
(B) of firearms other than destructive devices, a fee of $50 per year; or
(C) of ammunition for firearms, other than
ammunition for destructive devices or armor
piercing ammunition, a fee of $10 per year. (2) If the applicant is an importer—
(A) of destructive devices, ammunition for
destructive devices or armor piercing ammunition, a fee of $1,000 per year; or
(B) of firearms other than destructive devices or ammunition for firearms other than
destructive devices, or ammunition other than
armor piercing ammunition, a fee of $50 per
year.

chunks.content:
42
Torts
§ 426
Comment:
a. Collateral negligence. The negligence of a
contractor in the course of performing work entrusted
to him by his employer, which does not make the result
fall short of that which it would be the employer's duty
to attain, had he done the work himself, is collateral
negligence. Illustration:
1. A employs B, a competent contractor, to
excavate a cellar on land immediately adjoining a
public highway. The contract requires B to provide the fence necessary to prevent pedestrians
from falling into the excavation. A is liable to C,
a pedestrian, who falls into the excavation because the fence as erected by Bis flimsy or because B has not erected the fence as his contract
required. A is not liable to D, a pedestrian hurt
by the carelessness of B's workmen in handling
the timbers while they are erecting the fence
or by the careless handling of tools while so
doing. a. "Collateral negligence." The kind of negligence covered by
this Section, for which the employer is not liable, is commonly called
by the courts "collateral negligence," meaning negligence collateral to
the contemplated risk. Sometimes it is called "casual negligence." It
has sometimes been described as negligence in the operative detail of
the work, as distinguished from the general plan or method followed,
or the result to be accomplished.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
Frequently this distinction can be
made, since negligence in operative details will often not be within
the contemplation of the employer when the contract is made. The distinction is not, however, essentially one between operative detail and
general method. It is rather one of negligence which is unusual or
abnormal, or foreign to the normal or contemplated risks of doing the
work, as distinguished from negligence which creates only the normal
or contemplated risk. Thus an employer may hire a contractor to make an excavation,
reasonably expecting that the contractor will proceed in the normal
and usual manner with a bulldozer, or with pick and shovel. When the
contractor, for reasons of his own, decides to use blasting instead,
and the blasting is done in a negligent manner, so that it injures the
plaintiff, such negligence is "collateral" to the contemplated risk,
and the employer is not liable. If, on the other hand, the blasting

C. Equitable interests other than those under
a trust.
Donative transactions may result in the
creation of an equitable interest where the holder
of the legal title has no active responsibilities
and is purely a passive holder of the legal title.
Such an equitable interest is not an equitable
interest under a trust for the purposes of the rule
of this Section and a disabling restraint with
respect to such an equitable interest in invalid.
Illustration:
10. O, owning Blackacre in fee simple
absolute, makes an otherwise effective devise
thereof "to A and his heirs for the use of B and
his heirs, for the use of C and his heirs, but
C shall be unable to transfer in any manner his
interest in Blackacre to anyone. C has a use
on a use and the statute of uses does not convert
his equitable use estate into a legal fee simple.
B is the holder of the legal title in fee simple
and the disabling restraint on C's equitable fee
simple is invalid.

for, the negligence of the contractor with respect to all risks which
are inherent in the normal and usual manner of doing the work under the
particular circumstances. (See § 427). He is not required to contemplate or anticipate abnormal or unusual kinds of negligence on the part
of the contractor, or negligence in the performance of operative details
of the work which ordinarily may be expected to be carried out with proper care, unless the circumstances under which the work is done give him
warning of some special reason to take precautions, or some special risk
of harm to others arising from the work. Illustrations:
1. A employs B, an independent contractor, to excavate a cellar
on land abutting on a public highway. The contract requires the
contractor to provide a fence to prevent pedestrians from falling
into the excavation. B fails to erect the fance, or negligently
erects a fence so flimsy that it gives way when a pedestrian comes
in contact with it. As a result C, a pedestrian, falls into the
excavation and is injured. A is subject to liability to C. 2.

Under the facts stated in Illustration 1, a workman employed
by B to erect the fence negligently drops a hammer on the toe of C,
a passing pedestrian. This is "collateral negligence," and A is
not liable to C. 3. A employs B, an independent contractor, to paint a sign
suspended from A's building over the public sidewalk. A workman
employed by B negligently drops his paint bucket, so that it falls
upon C, a pedestrian. A is subject to liability to C. 4. A employs B, an independent contractor, to paint the inside
of a room on the second floor of his building. A workman employed
by B negligently sets his paint bucket on the window sill, and then
knocks it off, so that it falls upon C, a pedestrian in the street. This is "collateral negligence," and A is not liable to B. 5. A employs B, an independent contractor, to build a wall on
A's land. While the wall is under construction B's workmen negligently splash mortar over C's adjoining windows and the clothes
in her yard. A is subject to liability to C. 6. Under the facts stated in Illustration 5, B's workmen
splash mortar from a box on the ground into the eye of C, a passing pedestrian on the sidewalk. This is "collateral" negligence,
and A is not liable to C.

§ 427
Torts
44
427. NEGLIGENCE IN DOING INHERENTLY DAN
GEROUS WORK. One who employs an independent contractor
to do work which is inherently dangerous to others
is subject to liability for bodily harm caused to them
by the contractor's failure to exercise reasonable
care to prevent harm resulting from the dangerous
character of the work,
8427. NEGLIGENCE AS TO DANGER INHERENT IN THE WORK
ONE WHO EMPLOYS AN INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR TO DO WORK INVOLVING A
SPECIAL DANGER TO OTHERS WHICH THE EMPLOYER KNOWS OR HAS REASON TO KNOW
TO BE INHERENT IN OR NORMAL TO THE WORK, OR WHICH HE CONTEMPLATES OR
HAS REASON TO CONTEMPLATE WHEN MAKING THE CONTRACT, IS SUBJECT TO
LIABILITY FOR PHYSICAL HARM CAUSED TO SUCH OTHERS BY THE CONTRACTOR'S
FAILURE TO TAKE REASONABLE PRECAUTIONS AGAINST SUCH DANGER. Note to Institute: As to the close relation, or duplication, of
this Section and 416, see the Note under that Section. As to its
relation to the "collateral negligence" covered by 8 426, see the Note
there. Here the old Section and the Comment appear to be much too narrow. It is not a question of "inherently dangerous" work, but of danger inherent in the work.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
The basic idea appears in reality to be a danger
contemplated by the employer when the contract is made, as distinguished
from dangers resulting from the "collateral negligence" under § 426,
which the employer may reasonably assume will not arise. However, the
phrases customarily used in the decisions are "inherently dangerous"
and "intrinsically dangerous, and it seems desirable to make some use
of that language. The old Section, or at least the Comment, appears to have been drawn
with something like the "ultra-hazardous activity" in mind, with stress
on a high degree of risk and the necessity of special skill and care. The Explanatory Notes to Preliminary Draft No. 40 (1930), 53-57, cite
cases on blasting, the use of fire in clearing land, and the like. The
rule stated here is certainly broader than such activities. In Evans v. Elliott, (1941) 220 N.C. 253, 17 S.E. 2d 125, the court said, as to
"inherently dangerous" work under the rule here stated:
"The subject must not be confused with concepts of hazardous employment, usually involving a high degree of danger, since we are here dealing with danger which manifests itself to the general public. It is not
essential, to come under the rule, that the work should involve a major

Comment:
The
a. Meaning of "inherently dangerous."
words "inherently dangerous work" are used to indi
cate not only that the nature of the work itself, or of
the instrumentalities which must necessarily be used
in doing it, is such that it can only be safely performed
by the exercise of a special skill and care, as distinguished from work which can be safely done if performed with ordinary skill and care or is dangerous
irrespective of whether special skill or care is used, but
also that the work, if unskillfully and carelessly done,
involves a grave risk of serious bodily harm or death. The usual situations in which the liability stated
in this Section is imposed are those in which the work
in hand involves the use of instrumentalities, such as
fire or high explosives, which require constant attention and skillful management in order that they may
not be injurious to others or those in which the work
itself, like the demolition of a high chimney, is incapable of being safely done unless the persons who
do it are highly skilled and act with the utmost attention and care. The liability stated in this Section extends only to harm which is caused by the failure so to
act as to minimize to the uttermost the danger inherent
in the nature of the work or in the instrumentalities
used.

inherently dangerous. Thus, one who employs a contractor to do blasting close to a public highway or to
the land of another is liable under this Section if the
blasting is carelessly done or the explosives carelessly
handled by the contractor or his servants. He is not
liable if the driver of one of the contractor's carts
while conveying explosives to the place of work, carelessly runs over and injures a traveler upon a highway. So too, one who employs a contractor to demolish a high chimney or a wall made ruinous by a
fire, is liable under the rule stated in this Section for
the contractor's failure to use the utmost skill and
competence in preventing his work from causing the
building to fall upon an adjacent highway or land. He is not liable for harm caused to persons on the
adjacent highway or land by the carelessness of a
workman in dropping a tool.

a. The rule stated in this Section is closely related to, and to
a considerable extent a duplication of, that stated in § 416, as to
work likely to create a peculiar risk of harm to others unless special
precautions are taken. See Comment a under that Section. b. The rule stated in this Section is commonly expressed by the
courts in terms of liability of the employer for negligence of the contractor in doing work which is "inherently" or "intrinsically" dangerous. It is not, however, necessary to the employer's liability that the work
be of a kind which cannot be done without a risk of harm to others, or
that it be of a kind which involves a high degree of risk of such harm,
or that the risk be one of very serious harm, such as death or serious
bodily injury. It is not necessary that the work call for any special
skill or care in doing it. It is sufficient that work of any kind involves a risk, recognizable in advance, of physical harm to others which
is inherent in the work itself, or normally to be expected in the ordinary course of the usual or prescribed way of doing it, or that the employer has special reason to contemplate such a risk under the particular
circumstances under which the work is to be done. c.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
The rule stated applies where the work involves the use of instrumentalities, such as fire or high explosives, which require constant
attention and skillful management in order that they may not be harmful
to others. It applies also where such work as the demolition of a high
chimney is incapable of being done safely unless those who do it are
highly skilled and act with the utmost attention and care. It is not,
however, limited to such highly dangerous activities. The rule applies
equally to work which, although not highly dangerous, involves a risk
recognizable in advance that danger inherent in the work itself, or in
the ordinary or prescribed way of doing it, may cause harm to others. Thus an excavation in the highway, although it is not a highly dangerous
activity and calls for no special skill, involves a recognizable risk
that some one may fall into the excavation unless it is properly guarded. Likewise the use of a scaffold in painting the wall of a building above
the sidewalk involves a recognizable risk that the scaffold, paint brush
or bucket, or the painter himself, may fall and injure some one passing
below. d.

As in the case of the rule stated in § 416, the rule here stated
applies only where the harm results from the negligence of the contractor
in failing to take precautions against the danger involved in the work
itself, which the employer should contemplate at the time of his contract. It has no application where the negligence of the contractor creates a
new risk, not inherent in the work itself or in the ordinary or prescribed
way of doing it, and not reasonably to be contemplated by the employer. Likewise the rule stated here has no application to the "collateral"
negligence of the contractar covered in § 426, particularly as to negligence in the operative details of the work which involve no peculiar
risk, and which the employer may reasonably assume will be carried out
with proper care. The rule stated in § 426 is thus the converse of

ONE WHO EMPLOYS AN INDEPENDENT CONTRACTOR TO DO WORK WHICH THE

THE LAND OF ANOTHER OR THE CREATION OF A PUBLIC OR A PRIVATE NUISANCE,

$ 433A. APPORTIONMENT OF HARM TO CAUSES
(1) DAMAGES FOR ANY HARM WHICH IS SINGLE AND INDIVISIBLE CANNOT
BE APPORTIONED AMONG TWO OR MORE CAUSES. (2) DAMAGES FOR HARM ARE TO BE APPORTIONED AMONG TWO OR MORE
CAUSES WHERE
(a) THERE ARE DISTINCT HARMS; OR
(b)
THERE IS A REASONABLE BASIS FOR THE DIVISION OF A SINGLE HARM
ACCORDING TO THE CONTRIBUTION OF EACH CAUSE. Note to Institute: This Section brings forward the rules now stated
in §§ 875, 879 and 881, which are as follows:
$ 875. Except as stated in § 881, each of two or more persons whose
tortious conduct is a legal cause of a harm to another is liable to the
other for the entire harm. $879. Except as stated in § 881, each of two persons who is independently guilty of tortious conduct which is a substantial factor in
causing a harm to another is liable for the entire harm, in the absence
of a superseding cause. § 881. Where two or more persons, each acting independently, create or maintain a situation which is a tortious invasion of a landowner's
interest in the use and enjoyment of land by interfering with his quiet,
light, air or flowing water, each is liable only for such proportion of
the harm caused to the land or the loss of enjoyment of it by the owner
as his contribution to the harm bears to the total harm.

3. The rule stated in Subsection (2) is not limited to apportionment between joint tortfeasors. There may also be apportionment between
a tortfeasor and an innocent cause. Comment:
a. The rules stated in this Section apply whenever two or more causes have combined to bring about harm to the plaintiff, and each has been
a substantial factor in producing the harm, as stated in § 431 and § 433. They apply where each of the causes in question consists of the tortious
conduct of a person; and it is immaterial whether all or some of such
persons are joined as defendants in the particular action. The rules
stated apply also where one or more of the contributing causes is an
innocent one, as where the negligence of a defendant combines with the
innocent conduct of another person, or with the operation of a force of
nature, or with a pre-existing condition which the defendant has not
caused, to bring about the harm to the plaintiff. The rules stated apply
also where one of the causes in question is the conduct of the plaintiff
himself, whether it be negligent or innocent. Comment on Subsection (1):
b. Certain kinds of harm, by their very nature, are normally incapable of any logical, reasonable or practical division.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
Death is that
kind of harm, since it is impossible, except on a purely arbitrary basis
for the purpose of accomplishing the result, to say that one man has
caused half of it, and another the rest. The same is true of a broken
leg, or any single wound, or the destruction of a house by fire, or the
sinking of a barge. Such harms can be apportioned, if at all, only upon
the basis of a prior diminution in value of what has been destroyed, as
stated in 433B. By far the greater number of personal injuries, and
of harms to tangible property, are thus normally single and indivisible. Where two or more causes combine to produce such a single result, incapable of division on any logical or reasonable basis, and each is a
substantial factor in bringing about the harm, the courts have refused
to make an arbitrary apportionment for its own sake, and each of the
causes is charged with responsibility for the entire harm. The typical
case is that of two negligently driven vehicles which collide and kill a
bystander. The two drivers have not acted in concert, and the duties
which they owe to the plaintiff are separate and distinct, and may not
be identical in character or scope; but the entire liability of each
driver rests upon the obvious fact that each has caused the single result, and that no rational basis for division can be found.

c. Distinct harms. There are other results which, by their nature, are more capable of apportionment. If two defendants independently shoot the plaintiff at the same time, and one wounds him in the
arm and the other in the leg, the ultimate result may be a badly damaged
plaintiff in the hospital, but it is still possible, as a logical, reasonable and practical matter, to regard the two wounds as separate injuries, and as distinct wrongs. The mere coincidence in time does not
make the two wounds a single harm, or the conduct of the defendants
one tort. There may be difficulty in the apportionment of some elements of damages, such as the pain and suffering resulting from the
two wounds, or the medical expenses, but this does not mean that one
defendant must be liable for the distinct harm inflicted by the other. It is possible to make a rough estimate which will fairly apportion
such subsidiary elements of damages. d. Successive injuries. The harm inflicted may be conveniently
severable in point of time. Thus if two defendants, independently
operating the same plant, pollute a stream over successive periods,
it is clear that each has caused a separate amount of harm, limited in
time, and that neither has any responsibility for the harm caused by
the other.

wrongdoer may be liable for the entire damage, while the later one will
not. Thus an original tortfeasor may be liable not only for the harm
which he has himself inflicted, but also for the additional damages
resulting from the negligent treatment of the injury by a physician. (See $457). The physician, on the other hand, has played no part in
causing the original injury, and will be liable only for the additional
harm caused by his own negligence in treatment. There may be many other
cases in which the first wrongdoer is liable for the additional harm
caused by the intervening negligence of the later one, while the latter
is liable only for what he has himself caused. Пlustrations:

Comment:
a.
Rationale. The established policy of the law
is in favor of freedom of alienation. The basis for
the assumption that social welfare requires freedom of
alienation of property interests is discussed in the
Rationale of Part I of this Division and also in the
Introductory Note to Part II. This policy is particularly applicable when the restraint is imposed on
what is, or otherwise would be, an indefeasible legal
possessory interest, because the curtailment of the
power of alienation of such interests, totally or
partially, is the situation where the dangers of
restraints on alienation were first encountered.
To uphold restraints on the alienation of such
interests it must appear that the objective sought
to be accomplished by the imposition of the restraint is of sufficient social importance to outweigh the evils which flow from interfering with the
power of alienation, or that the curtailment of the
power of alienation is so slight that no social
danger is involved.

In such cases, where the restraint
is designed to operate against the combined action
of the concurrent owners, no different considerations
exist than when the restraint is imposed on an ownership in severalty of the same type of interest.
When, however, the restraint is sought to be imposed
with respect to the action of each separate owner as
to his or her own share, different considerations
must be evaluated.
The interest of one concurrent
owner is not as marketable an interest as an interest
of the same type owned in severalty. People are less
willing to purchase an interest in property when
the management of it must be shared with some other
concurrent owner, than when they have the sole
management. Thus, a restraint operative as to one
concurrent owner's share is an interference with the
alienation of an interest which, apart from the restraint, is not as alienable as an interest in severalty. The difference, however, is not sufficient
to change the applicability of the rules as to
restraints on alienation.

chunks.content:
The usual purpose of a restraint operative as
to the share of a concurrent owner is to avoid the
danger of having to share the concurrent interest
with some undesirable person, and thereby assure
harmony among the concurrent owners. This
objective can only be accomplished, however, where
a similar restraint would be valid on an interest
in severalty.
A legal incident of one type of concurrent
ownership, a tenancy by the entireties, may be that
the interest of neither the husband nor the wife
is alienable separately, but both interests can
be alienated together. No problem of restraints
on alienation is presented in connection with such
concurrent estate unless the restraint attempts
to prevent the alienation of the interests of
both husband and wife when they join in the conveyance.

d. Application-Unqualified restraints. An unqualified restraint on what is, or otherwise would
be, an indefeasible possessory interest is an attempt
to prevent perpetually the alienation of the interest
to all persons and by all available methods (see
Illustration 1). The objectives which one imposing
such an extensive restraint on alienation could have
in mind are never regarded as sufficiently meritorious
to outweigh the evils which such interference with
the power of alienation would cause.
If the unqualified restraint is a forfeiture
restraint and the property is to pass to a person
other than the original transferor when the restraint
is violated, the gift over may violate the rule against
perpetuities.
[Subsection (3)]. Thus an additional
ground may exist to aid in the elimination of the
unqualified restraint.

chunks.content:
§ 433B
Torts
66
$ 433B. POTENTIAL HARM FROM OTHER CAUSE
WHERE AN INNOCENT CAUSE ALREADY IN OPERATION HAS AFFECTED THE
VALUE OF THE PLAINTIFF'S INTEREST BY MAKING IT HIGHLY PROBABLE THAT
HARM TO IT WILL OCCUR, AND HARM TO THAT INTEREST IS THEN IN FACT
CAUSED BY THE TORTIOUS CONDUCT OF THE DEFENDANT, HE IS SUBJECT TO
LIABILITY ONLY FOR THE REDUCED VALUE OF THE INTEREST. Comment:
a. The rule stated in this Section is a special application of
the rule stated in Subsection (2) of § 433A. It deals with the apportionment of an otherwise indivisible harm, upon the basis of potential
harm from an innocent cause already in operation, which has reduced
the value of the interest in fact harmed by the tortious conduct of
the defendant. b. The rule applies only where the innocent cause is already in
operation, and the threatened harm is so highly probable, and so imminent, as to affect the value of the plaintiff's interest. Thus if the
plaintiff is standing in the path of an avalanche when the defendant
shoots and kills him, the value of his life is already reduced by the
substantial certainty of his death from the avalanche, and the liability of the defendant is limited accordingly. It is otherwise where
the plaintiff is killed as he is about to embark on a steamship which
is doomed to strike an iceberg ten days later and sink with everyone on
board.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
In such a case his life has full value at the time he is killed,
as any insurance company would agree. So likewise a forest fire a hundred yards away will affect the market value of a building which the
defendant destroys with dynamite, while a fire a hundred miles away
will not, even though it may later burn over the site of the building. And the fact that death is the inevitable ultimate lot of all mankind
does not subtract from the liability of one who kills another, including any liability for funeral expenses. C. The rule stated in this Section applies only where the loss in
value because of the potential harm has occurred solely through the
operation of the innocent cause, and by reason of the harm which it
threatens. It has no application where the tortious conduct of the
defendant himself has contributed to bring about the loss in value by
threatening the same harm. Illustrations:
1. A is dying of an incurable cancer, which is certain to
kill him in a month. B negligently shoots and kills A. B's
liability is limited to the value of a month of A's life.

Decisions are lacking as
to the possible application of the rule stated in this Section to potential harm from another cause which is not innocent in its origin, but
is set in operation by the tortious conduct of a third person. The
problem may be illustrated by supposing that A negligently administers
to B a slow poison, for which there is no known antidote, and which is
certain to kill B in three days. Five minutes later C negligently
shoots B and kills him. In such a case it is arguable that C has deprived B not only of
three days of life, but also of a potential cause of action against A
for killing him, and therefore that the rule stated in this Section
should not apply. In other words, in such a case, C should be subject
to liability for the full value of B's life, on the basis of his normal
life expectancy. In the absence of decisions upon the point, however,
the Institute expresses no opinion on the matter.

INTENDED TO CAUSE HARM, AND IT IS PROVED THAT HARM HAS BEEN CAUSED
TO THE PLAINTIFF BY ONLY ONE OF THEM, BUT THERE IS UNCERTAINTY AS TO
WHICH ONE HAS CAUSED IT, THE BURDEN IS UPON EACH SUCH ACTOR TO PROVE
THAT HE HAS NOT CAUSED THE HARM. Caveat: The Institute expresses no opinion as to whether the
rule stated in Subsection (3) is to be applied to actors whose conduct
is tortious only in that it would involve strict liability for harm
which it has caused. Comment on Subsection (1):
a. Subsection (1) states the general rule as to the burden of
proof on the issue of causation. As on other issues in civil cases,
the plaintiff is required to produce evidence that the conduct of the
defendant has been a substantial factor in bringing about the harm he
has suffered, and to sustain his burden of proof by a preponderance of
the evidence.

it becomes the duty of the court to direct a verdict for the defendant. Illustrations:

trauma in producing cancer is still a matter of medical speculation and uncertainty. On this evidence, A has not sustained his
burden of proof as to B's causation of the cancer.

a reasonable doubt. He is not required to eliminate entirely all possibility that the defendant's tortious conduct was not a cause. It is enough
that he introduces evidence from which reasonable men may conclude that
it is more probable that the event was caused by the defendant than that
it was not. The fact of causation is incapable of mathematical proof,
since no man can say with absolute certainty what would have occurred if
the defendant had acted otherwise. If, as a matter of ordinary experience,
a particular act or omission might be expected to produce a particular
result, and if that result has in fact followed, the conclusion may be
justified that the causal relation exists.

C. Subsection (2) states an exception to the general rule stated
in Subsection (1). It arises where the tortious conduct of two or more
actors combines to bring about harm to the plaintiff, and the harm
which results is capable of apportionment among the causes producing
it, as stated in § 433A (2), and the Comments to that Section. A typical case is the pollution of a stream by a number of factories which
discharge impurities into it. It is not essential to the application
of the rule stated in Subsection (2) that all of the tortfeasors who
will become liable for some part of the apportioned damages be joined

The reason for the exceptional rule placing the burden of
proof as to apportionment upon the defendant or defendants is the
injustice of allowing a proved wrongdoer who has in fact caused some
harm to the plaintiff to escape liability merely because the harm
which he has inflicted has combined with similar harm inflicted by
other wrongdoers, and the nature of the harm itself has made it necessary that evidence be produced before it can be apportioned. In such
a case the defendant may justly be required to assume the burden of
producing that evidence, or if he is not able to do so, of bearing
the full responsibility. As between the proved tortfeasor who has
clearly caused some harm, and the entirely innocent plaintiff, any
hardship due to lack of evidence as to the extent of the harm caused
should fall upon the former. e. In order for the rule stated in Subsection (2) to apply, it

combined with that of others to bring about harm of a character which

made it difficult or impossible to prove which of them is responsible. h. The rule stated in Subsection (3) applies only where it is
proved that each of two or more actors has been negligent or has intended to cause the harm, and that the harm has resulted from the conduct of some one of them. On these issues the plaintiff still has the
burden of proof. The rule rule stated has no application to cases of
alternative liability, where there is no proof that the conduct of more
than one actor has been negligent or intentional at all. In such a
case the plaintiff has the burden of proof both as to the tortious
conduct and as to the causal relation. The cases thus far decided in which the rule stated in Subsection (3) has been applied all have been cases in which all of the actors
involved have been joined as defendants. All of them have involved conduct simultaneous in time, or substantially so, and all of them have
involved conduct of substantially the same character, creating substantially the same risk of harm, on the part of each actor.

stated in Subsection (2) may apply where bodily harm to the other results

The only possible justification for a special rule in the case of
the telegraph company appears to be the special responsibility to the
public undertaken by the public utility. The federal rule, which controls as to interstate messages, denies recovery for mental suffering
without physical consequences. Western Union Tel. Co. v. Speight
The Advisers and the Council have agreed with the Reporter that
the exception should not be stated. In addition to the fact that it
is a minority rule in the absence of statute, the reason for rejecting
it is that the federal rule should be accepted, in order to avoid the
absurdity of making recovery turn upon whether the message crosses a
state line. Comment:
a. The rule stated in this Section stands in contrast to those
stated in $ 436, under which an actor who has created an unreasonable
risk of causing either bodily harm or emotional disturbance to another
becomes subject to liability for bodily harm brought about solely by
the internal operation of emotional disturbance. Under the rule stated in this Section, the actor is not liable when his negligent conduct results in the emotional disturbance alone, without the bodily
harm or other compensable damage.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
The difference is one between the
negligent automobile driver who narrowly misses a woman and frightens
her into a miscarriage, and the negligent driver who merely frightens
her, without more. b. The reasons for the distinction, as usually stated by the
courts, have been three. One is that emotional disturbance which is
not so severe or serious as to have physical consequences, is normally
in the realm of the trivial, and so falls within the maxim that the
law does not concern itself with trifles. It is likely to be so
temporary, so evanescent, and so relatively harmless and unimportant,
that the task of compensating for it would unduly burden the courts
and the defendants. The second is that in the absence of the guarantee of genuineness provided by resulting bodily harm, such emotional
disturbance is too easily feigned, depending, as it must, very largely
upon the subjective testimony of the plaintiff; and that to allow recovery for it would open too wide a door for false claimants who have
suffered no real harm at all. The third is that where the defendant
has been merely negligent, without any element of intent to do harm,
his fault is not so great that he should be required to make good a
purely mental disturbance. c. The rule stated in this Section applies to all forms of emotional disturbance, including fright, nervous shock, nausea, grief,
rage, and humiliation.

$442A. INTERVENING FORCE RISKED BY ACTOR'S CONDUCT
WHERE THE NEGLIGENT CONDUCT OF THE ACTOR CREATES OR INCREASES
THE FORESEEABLE RISK OF HARM THROUGH THE INTERVENTION OF ANOTHER
FORCE, AND IS A SUBSTANTIAL FACTOR IN CAUSING THE HARM, SUCH INTER-
VENTION IS NOT A SUPERSEDING CAUSE. Note to Institute:
See § 443. That Section has been split into
two parts, leaving "normal" intervening forces under § 443. The rule
stated here is the one commonly stated by the courts. Comment:
a. The rule stated in this Section applies to any intervening
force, whether it be a force of nature, or the act of a human being,
or of an animal. b. Where the negligence of the actor has created the risk of harm
to another, because of the likelihoos of such intervention, the actor is
not relieved of responsibility merely because the risk which he has
created has in fact been fulfilled. The same is true where there is
already some existing risk or possibility of the intervention, but the
negligence of the actor has increased the risk of such intervention,
or of harm if it occurs. Illustration:
1. In the month of December A ships potatoes in an unheated
car of B Railroad through the state of Maine. B Railroad negligently delays the shipment in Maine for three days, thereby increasing the already existing risk that the potatoes will be
damaged by the cold.

$442B. INTERVENING FORCE CAUSING SAME HARM AS THAT RISKED BY THE
ACTOR'S CONDUCT
WHERE THE ACTOR'S CONDUCT CREATES OR INCREASES THE RISK OF A
PARTICULAR HARM, AND IS A SUBSTANTIAL FACTOR IN CAUSING THAT HARM,
THE FACT THAT THE HARM IS BROUGHT ABOUT THROUGH THE INTERVENTION OF
ANOTHER FORCE DOES NOT RELIEVE THE ACTOR OF LIABILITY, EXCEPT WHERE
THAT FORCE IS THE INTENTIONALLY TORTIOUS OR CRIMINAL ACT OF A THIRD
PERSON. Comment:
a. The rule stated in this Section is a special application of
the principle stated in § 435 (1), that the fact that the actor neither
foresaw nor could have foreseen the manner in which a particular harm
is brought about does not prevent his liability where the other conditions necessary to it exist. Compare Illustration 1 under that Section. b. If the actor's conduct has created or increased the risk that
a particular harm to the plaintiff will occur, and has been a substantial factor in causing that harm, it is immaterial to the actor's liability that the harm is brought about in a manner which no one in his
position could possibly have been expected to foresee or anticipate.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23

persons which are not intentionally tortious or criminal. This is to
say that any harm which is in itself foreseeable, as to which the actor
has created or increased the recognizable risk, is always "proximate,"
no matter how it is brought about, except where there is such intentionally tortious or criminal intervention. Пlustrations:

§ 452. THIRD PERSON'S FAILURE TO PREVENT
HARM. Failure of a third person to perform a duty
owing to another to protect him from harm threatened by the actor's negligent conduct is not a superseding cause of the other's harm. (1) EXCEPT AS STATED IN SUBSECTION (2), THE FAILURE OF A
THIRD PERSON TO ACT TO PREVENT HARM TO ANOTHER THREATENED BY THE
ACTOR'S NEGLIGENT CONDUCT IS NOT A SUPERSEDING CAUSE OF SUCH HARM. (2) WHERE, BY CONTRACT OR OTHERWISE, ALL RESPONSIBILITY FOR
THE PROTECTION OF THE OTHER AGAINST THE THREATENED HARM IS SHIFTED
TO THE THIRD PERSON, HIS INTENTIONAL OR NEGLIGENT FAILURE TO ACT
TO PREVENT SUCH HARM IS A SUPERSEDING CAUSE. Note to Institute: This Section has been changed by the addition
of Subsection (2). Neither the Advisers nor the Council have been able
to suggest better language. The Subsection appears necessary to cover a group of cases, in
substantial number, in which the failure of a third person to act has
been held to relieve the original actor of liability. The old analysis
of these cases was in terms of "termination of the risk." This appears
to be clearly the wrong approach. The risk is not terminated. The
danger created by the actor is still alive, and the plaintiff is in
fact injured by that danger.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23

is that he has been relieved of responsibility for the risk, which is
shifted to the third person. It appears to be impossible to state any rule as to when such
responsibility is shifted. Various factors enter in: contract or
express agreement, lapse of time, the relation between the actor and
the third person, the relation between the third person and the plaintiff, the customs of the community in various types of situations, and
no doubt many others. Apparently the best that can be done is to make
a general statement as in Subs ection (2), and rely upon Comments and
Illustrations to indicate what is meant. The following cases indicate the problem:
Goar v. Village of Stephen (1923) 157 Minn. 228, 196 N.W. 171. Defendant electric company installed a transformer pole for the Village. The contract provided that the Village would assume all responsibility
for inspection and maintenance of the pole. Two wires on the pole were
set too close together, and over a period of 17 months the "more or

Red River Valley" rubbed the wires together, and wore off the insula-
