Comment:
a. The situation covered by both parts of this Section is that
in which, after the original actor has been negligent, and so has created an unreasonable risk of harm to another, a third person has the
opportunity, by taking affirmative action, to avert the threatened
harm. This implies that if such action were taken, it would prevent
the negligence of the original actor from causing the harm which has
in fact resulted. Comment on Subsection (1):
b. Subsection (1) states the rule applicable in the ordinary case,
that the failure of the third person to act to prevent harm to the other,
threatened by the original actor's negligent conduct, is not a superseding cause of such harm, and so does not relieve the actor of liability
for the harm which he has in fact caused. If the third person is under
a duty to the other to take such action, his failure to do so will subject him to liability for his own negligence, which is concurrent with
that of the actor, for the resulting harm which he has failed to prevent; but his failure to perform his duty does not relieve the original
actor of liability for the results of his own negligence.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
A fortiori,
where the third person is under no duty to the other to take any action,
but merely has the opportunity to do so, his failure to act not only
does not make him liable, but is not a superseding cause which will
relieve the original actor of liability. As to the exceptional cases
in which all responsibility has been shifted to the third person, see
Comments on Subsection (2). C. The rule stated in Subsection (1) applies not only where the
third person makes no effort to act to avert the harm, but also where
he makes such an affort, but the action which he takes is insufficient,
or is otherwise unsuccessful, in averting the harm. Illustrations:
1. A, the owner of a house abutting on a street in B City,
employs C to dig a trench across the highway to make a connection
with a sewer. C does the work of replacing the sidewalk so negligently that it is left in a condition dangerous for travel. A
knows of this, and B City is notified, but neither takes any
steps to put the sidewalk in safe condition. Several weeks after
C has completed the work D, walking on the sidewalk at night, and
without any negligence of his own, is hurt by a fall resulting
from the bad condition of the sidewalk. The failure of A, and
of B City, to have the sidewalk repaired, make both subject to
liability to D, but are not superseding causes relieving C of
liability to D.

C. D, the daughter of C, attempts to light a fire with the kerosene. Because of the presence of gasoline, an explosion ensues by
which C is so severely injured that he dies. The fact that B was
negligent in not seeing to it that the gasoline was effectively
removed does not prevent A from being liable for the death of C. 3. The A Railroad Company negligently sets fire to the timber
land of B, in a state in which, at common law or by statute, it is
the duty of a landowner to use reasonable care to prevent a fire,
no matter how set, from spreading to adjacent land. B, knowing
that the fire has been set, either makes no effort to prevent its
spread, or fails to exercise reasonable care in making his efforts
effectual. The fire spreads to the land of C. The failure of B
to perform his duty is not a superseding cause which relieves the
A Railroad Company from liability to C. 4.

An automobile negligently driven by A strikes B, and leaves
him on the highwaym unconscious and slowly bleeding to death. C,
a passing motorist, stops, looks over the situation, and decides to
drive on without doing anything to aid B. B bleeds to death. Regardless of whether C is under any duty to B to render such aid,
his failure to do so is not a superseding cause which will relieve
A of liability for the death of B. Comment on Subsection (2):
d. Subsection (2) covers the exceptional cases in which, because
the entire responsibility for the situation has been shifted to a third
person, the original actor is relieved of liability for the result which
follows from the operation of his own negligence. The shifted responsibility means in effect that the duty of obligation of the original actor
in the matter has terminated, and has been replaced by that of the third
person. e. One way in which the responsibility may be shifted is by contract between the actor and the third person. By express agreement, or
by fair implication from what is agreed, it may be understood that the
third person has taken over full responsibility for the situation, and
that the actor is relieved of his obligation. In many cases this is
not possible, since there are duties and obligations which cannot be
delegated or shifted to another.

f. Even in the absence of any contract or agreement, the circumstances may be such that the court will find that all responsibility
for the prevention of the harm has passed to the third person. It is
apparently impossible to state any comprehensive rule as to when such
a decision will be made. Various factors will enter into it. Among
them are the degree of danger and the magnitude of the risk of harm:
the character and position of the third person who is to take the responsibility, his knowledge of the danger, and the likelihood that he
will or will not exercise proper care, his relation to the plaintiff
or to the defendant, the lapse of time, and perhaps other considerations. The most that can be stated here is that when, by reason of
the interplay of such factors, the court finds that full responsibility
for control of the situation and prevention of the threatened harm has
passed to the third person, his failure to act is then a superseding
cause, which will relieve the original actor of liability. Illustrations:
1. The A Railroad negligently turns over to its connecting
carrier B Railroad a freight car, the door of which is in defective and dangerous condition. B Railroad operates the car on its
own line over a period of six months, during which time it negligently fails to inspect the car and discover the defect.

it to C, who is ignorant of the danger. While C is driving the
car the hood flies up, and C is injured. A is not liable to C.

Other defeasible estates in fee simple, which are
within the rule stated in this Section, as a practical

restraint on alienation is involved. This is true
whenever the event which defeats the estate is as

during the time that the estate remains defeasible.

develop into an estate in fee simple absolute, the
policy in favor of freedom of alienation requires
that restraints on alienation be kept within the same
limits as have been marked out for other types of

$4.3
POSSESSORY ESTATES IN FEE SIMPLE
CONDITIONAL AND FEE TAIL
A promissory restraint on alienation or a forfeiture restraint on alienation in a donative transfer
imposed on a possessory estate in fee simple conditional
or in fee tail is invalid to the extent that it abridges
the power in the estate holder to defeat the right of
the heirs of the body to inherit the property or abridges
the power to eliminate any future interest dependent
on the extinction of the descendant line of the estate
holder; to the extent such power is not abridged by such
restraint, the restraint is valid if, and only if, a
similar restraint on what is, or otherwise would be,
an indefeasible possessory interest in property is
valid under the rule stated in $4.1.
Comment:
a.
Cross-references.
All of the Comments
on the rule stated in $4.1 apply also when under the
rule stated in this Section, the rule stated in $4.1
is applicable.

QUESTIONS ON TENTATIVE DRAFT NO. 9
SUGGESTED FOR DISCUSSION AT ANNUAL MEETING
§ 433C. A new Section, dealing with the burden of proof on the
issue of causation in fact, and on the issues of apportionment raised
by § 433A. Cases are lacking on the issue of strict liability, raised by
the Caveat, and, as suggested in the Comments, there are other
problems likely to arise which have not been dealt with. Is this
handled satisfactorily? § 436. Subsection (3), and the Caveat, raise again the troublesome question of fright or shock at peril or harm to a third person. Have we reached the right result? § 436A. A new Section, dealing with negligence resulting in
mental disturbance alone. This is nowhere in the first Restatement,
and it obviously should be covered. What is to be done about the
cases of telegraph messages, discussed in the Note under this Section? § 442B. Another new Section, dealing with the situation where
the intervening force brings about the same result as that originally
risked. It appears to be amply supported by the cases. Is it
approved? $483. This deals with contributory negligence as a defense where
the defendant has violated a statute. The language is changed to place
the entire responsibility upon the defendant. Is this right? § 485. The "general rule" is reversed, to state that contributory
negligence is not imputed, with exceptions.

§§ 496A to 496G. These Sections add a new Chapter, dealing
with the defense of assumption of risk. This defense was first omitted
in the old Restatement, then inserted in very abbreviated form in a
last minute Section at the end of Volume IV. The proposed seven Sections have been the subject of prolonged
and lively dispute among the Advisers, which occupied the major
part of one of their meetings, led to a subsequent symposium in the
Louisiana Law Review, and among the combatants has acquired the
name of the Battle of the Wilderness. Eight of the Advisers disagree
with the Reporter, and want to strike out all of this Chapter except
perhaps the Section on express assumption of risk (§ 496B). The
Reporter stands his ground. Long memoranda have been submitted
for the consideration of the Council and the Institute, with a reply. from the Reporter and a rejoinder from Dean Wade. All concerned
regret the length to which all this has run; but since there is a genuine
difference of opinion, it has seemed desirable to set it all forth. Here the Reporter must appear frankly as a partisan, with the
support of only five out of thirteen of the Advisory Group. He has,
however, the unanimous support of the Council.

below the minimum altitudes prescribed by federal regulation. i. In 1946, in United States v. Causby, 328 U.S. 256, 66 S. Ct. 1062, 90 L. Ed. 1206, the Supreme Court declared that federal statutes,
together with administrative regulations adopted pursuant to them, had
the effect of making the upper air, above the prescribed minimum altitudes of flight, a public highway. The decision has been held to supersede state law on the matter, so that liability for entry into the air
space henceforth becomes a matter of federal law. So far as aviation
is concerned, private rights in the upper air no longer exist. j. In the Causby Case the court went on to say that if the landowner is to have full enjoyment of the land, he must have "exclusive
control of the immediate reaches of the enveloping atmosphere," and
"invasions of it are in the same category as invasions of the surface."
The effect of this is clearly to preserve the action of trespass as
a remedy where the "immediate reaches" are invaded by flight. k.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23

The actual holding in the Causby Case was that the rights of
the landowner were invaded, and there was a wrongful "taking" of his
property, when the flights into the "immediate reaches" of the air space
interfered with his use of the land. Subsequent federal cases have
limited the trespass liability to such cases, so that, even though
there is a flight below the prescribed minimum altitude, there is no
trespass unless there is such interference with actual, as distinguished
from potential, use. 1. "Immediate reaches" of the land has been defined to mean that
"the aircraft flights were at such altitudes as to interfere substantially with the landowner's possession and use of the airspace above
the surface." No more definite line can be drawn than is suggested
by the word "immediate." In the ordinary case, flight at 500 feet or
more above the surface is not within the "immediate reaches," while
flight within 50 feet, which interferes with actual use, clearly is,
and flight within 150 feet, which also so interferes, may present a
question of fact. m. Even though the flight is not within the "immediate reaches"
of the air space, it may still unreasonably interfere with the use and
enjoyment of the land. In such a case, the liability will rest upon

EACH SUCH ACTOR. (3) WHERE THE CONDUCT OF TWO OR MORE ACTORS IS NEGLIGENT OR
INTENDED TO CAUSE HARM, AND IT IS PROVED THAT HARM HAS BEEN CAUSED
TO THE PLAINTIFF BY ONLY ONE OF THEM, BUT THERE IS UNCERTAINTY AS TO
WHICH ONE HAS CAUSED IT, THE BURDEN IS UPON EACH SUCH ACTOR TO PROVE
THAT HE HAS NOT CAUSED THE HARM. Caveat: The Institute expresses no opinion as to whether the rule
stated in Subsection (3) is to be applied to actors whose conduct is
tortious only in that it would involve strict liability for harm which
it has caused. Note to Institute: The Council, by a vote of 12 to 10, recommends
the omission of the Caveat. Comment on Subsection (1):
This
a. Subsection (1) states the general rule as to the burden of proof
on the issue of causation.

chunks.content:
As on other issues in civil cases, the plaintiff is required to produce evidence that the conduct of the defendant has
been a substantial factor in bringing about the harm he has suffered, and
to sustain his burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence. means that he must make it appear that it is more likely than not that the
conduct of the defendant was a substantial factor in bringing about the
harm. A mere possibility of such causation is not enough; and when the
matter remains one of pure speculation or conjecture, or the probabilities
are at best evenly balanced, it becomes the duty of the court to direct a
verdict for the defendant. Illustrations:
1. Through the negligence of A, B suffers a slight cut on his
forehead from broken glass. Two years later a cancer develops at
the point of the cut. In A's action against B, the medical evidence
is that the cause of cancer is unknown; that it is possible that a
cut may be a substantial factor in producing cancer, since in some
comparatively rare cases cancers do develop at such a point of injury;
that most cuts do not lead to cancer, and most cancers develop without
any history of such injury; and that the effect of trauma in producing
cancer is still a matter of medical speculation and uncertainty. this evidence, A has not sustained his burden of proof as to B's causation of the cancer.

As in the case of Subsection (2), the reason for the exception is the
injustice of permitting proved wrongdoers, who among them have inflicted an injury upon the entirely innocent plaintiff, to escape liability
merely because the nature of their conduct and the resulting harm has
made it difficult or impossible to prove which of them is responsible. h. The rule stated in Subsection (3) applies only where it is
proved that each of two or more actors has been negligent or has intended to cause the harm, and that the harm has resulted from the conduct of some one of them. On these issues the plaintiff still has the
burden of proof. The rule rule stated has no application to cases of
alternative liability, where there is no proof that the conduct of more
than one actor has been negligent or intentional at all. In such a
case the plaintiff has the burden of proof both as to the tortious
conduct and as to the causal relation. The cases thus far decided in which the rule stated in Subsection (3) has been applied all have been cases in which all of the actors
involved have been joined as defendants. All of them have involved conduct simultaneous in time, or substantially so, and all of them have
involved conduct of substantially the same character, creating substantially the same risk of harm, on the part of each actor.

which they have created. Since such cases have not arisen, and the

11. Over a period of three years A successively stores his furniture in warehouses operated by B, C and D. At the end of that time A
finds that his piano has been damaged by a large dent in one corner. The nature of the dent indicates that it was caused by careless handling on a single occasion. A has the burden of proving whether the dent
was caused by the negligence of B, C or D. Comment on Caveat:
i. All of the cases thus far decided in which the rule stated in
Subsection (3) has been applied have been cases in which the conduct of
each actor was proved to have been negligent. The decisions all have
laid stress upon the established fault of each actor, together with the
proved fact that the harm to the plaintiff has resulted from the fault
of some one of them, as a reason for applying the rule. For this reason it appears clear that the same rule is to be applied in cases in
which it is proved that the conduct of the actor has been intended to
cause the harm. Cases are as yet lacking in which any auqestion has arisen of the
application of the rule to actors whose conduct is tortious in character only because it would subject the actor to strict liability for
harm which it is proved to have caused.

resulting damage to the dwelling. Suppose further that as a result
of the blasting a very valuable Ming porcelain vase is knocked from

and as the result of a single blast. Either actor, in other words,
could have caused the result, and one did so, but there is uncertainty as to which one. In the absence of decisions throwing light upon the matter, the
Institute expresses no opinion as to whether the rule stated in Subsection (3) is to be applied in such a case.

$436. PHYSICAL HARM RESULTING FROM EMO-
TIONAL DISTURBANCE. (1) If the actor's conduct is negligent as violating a duty of care designed to protect another
from a fright or other emotional disturbance which
the actor should recognize as involving an unreasonable risk of bodily harm, the fact that the harm
results solely through the internal operation of the
fright or other emotional disturbance does not protect the actor from liability. (2) If the actor's conduct is negligent as creating an unreasonable risk of causing bodily harm
to another otherwise than by subjecting him to

solely from the internal operation of fright or other
emotional disturbance does not protect the actor
from liability. (3) THE RULE STATED IN SUBSECTION (2) APPLIES WHERE THE BODILY
HARM TO THE OTHER RESULTS FROM HIS SHOCK OR FRIGHT AT HARM OR PERIL
TO A MEMBER OF HIS IMMEDIATE FAMILY OCCURRING IN HIS PRESENCE.

defendant, by his negligence, has endangered the plaintiff's own
safety and threatened him with bodily harm, so that the defendant
is in breach of an original duty to the plaintiff to exercise care

The only possible justification for a special rule in the case of
the telegraph company appears to be the special responsibility to the
public undertaken by the public utility. The federal rule, which controls as to interstate messages, denies recovery for mental suffering
without physical consequences. Western Union Tel. Co. v. Speight
The Advisers and the Council have agreed with the Reporter that
the exception should not be stated. In addition to the fact that it
is a minority rule in the absence of statute, the reason for rejecting
it is that the federal rule should be accepted, in order to avoid the
absurdity of making recovery turn upon whether the message crosses a
state line. Comment:
a. The rule stated in this Section stands in contrast to those
stated in 436, under which an actor who has created an unreasonable
risk of causing either bodily harm or emotional disturbance to another
becomes subject to liability for bodily harm brought about solely by
the internal operation of emotional disturbance. Under the rule stated in this Section, the actor is not liable when his negligent conduct results in the emotional disturbance alone, without the bodily
harm or other compensable damage.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
The difference is one between the
negligent automobile driver who narrowly misses a woman and frightens
her into a miscarriage, and the negligent driver who merely frightens
her, without more. b. The reasons for the distinction, as usually stated by the
courts, have been three. One is that emotional disturbance which is
not so severe or serious as to have physical consequences, is normally
in the realm of the trivial, and so falls within the maxim that the
law does not concern itself with trifles. It is likely to be so
temporary, so evanescent, and so relatively harmless and unimportant,
that the task of compensating for it would unduly burden the courts
and the defendants. The second is that in the absence of the guarantee of genuineness provided by resulting bodily harm, such emotional
disturbance is too easily feigned, depending, as it must, very largely
upon the subjective testimony of the plaintiff; and that to allow recovery for it would open too wide a door for false claimants who have
suffered no real harm at all. The third is that where the defendant
has been merely negligent, without any element of intent to do harm,
his fault is not so great that he should be required to make good a
purely mental disturbance. C. The rule stated in this Section applies to all forms of emotional disturbance, including fright, nervous shock, nausea, grief,
rage, and humiliation.

S442A. INTERVENING FORCE RISKED BY ACTOR'S CONDUCT
WHERE THE NEGLIGENT CONDUCT OF THE ACTOR CREATES OR INCREASES
THE FORESEEABLE RISK OF HARM THROUGH THE INTERVENTION OF ANOTHER
FORCE, AND IS A SUBSTANTIAL FACTOR IN CAUSING THE HARM, SUCH INTER-
VENTION IS NOT A SUPERSEDING CAUSE. Note to Institute: See § 443. That Section has been split into
two parts, leaving "normal" intervening forces under § 443. The rule
stated here is the one commonly stated by the courts. Comment:
a. The rule stated in this Section applies to any intervening
force, whether it be a force of nature, or the act of a human being,
or of an animal. b. Where the negligence of the actor has created the risk of harm
to another, because of the likelihoos of such intervention, the actor is
not relieved of responsibility merely because the risk which he has
created has in fact been fulfilled. The same is true where there is
already some existing risk or possibility of the intervention, but the
negligence of the actor has increased the risk of such intervention,
or of harm if it occurs. Illustration:
1. In the month of December A ships potatoes in an unheated
car of B Railroad through the state of Maine. B Railroad negligently delays the shipment in Maine for three days, thereby increasing the already existing risk that the potatoes will be
damaged by the cold.

$442B. INTERVENING FORCE CAUSING SAME HARM AS THAT RISKED BY THE
ACTOR'S CONDUCT
WHERE THE ACTOR'S CONDUCT CREATES OR INCREASES THE RISK OF A
PARTICULAR HARM, AND IS A SUBSTANTIAL FACTOR IN CAUSING THAT HARM,
THE FACT THAT THE HARM IS BROUGHT ABOUT THROUGH THE INTERVENTION OF
ANOTHER FORCE DOES NOT RELIEVE THE ACTOR OF LIABILITY, EXCEPT WHERE
THAT FORCE IS THE INTENTIONALLY TORTIOUS OR CRIMINAL ACT OF A THIRD
PERSON. Comment:
a. The rule stated in this Section is a special application of
the principle stated in § 435 (1), that the fact that the actor neither
foresaw nor could have foreseen the manner in which a particular harm
is brought about does not prevent his liability where the other conditions necessary to it exist. Compare Illustration 1 under that Section. b. If the actor's conduct has created or increased the risk that
a particular harm to the plaintiff will occur, and has been a substantial factor in causing that harm, it is immaterial to the actor's liability that the harm is brought about in a manner which no one in his
position could possibly have been expected to foresee or anticipate.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
This is true not only where the result is produced by the direct operation of the actor's conduct upon conditions or circumstances existing
at the time, but also where it is brought about through the intervention of other forces which the actor could not have expected, whether
they be forces of nature, or the actions of animals, or those of third
persons which are not intentionally tortious or criminal. This is to
say that any harm which is in itself foreseeable, as to which the actor
has created or increased the recognizable risk, is always "proximate,"
no matter how it is brought about, except where there is such intentionally tortious or criminal intervention. Пlustrations:
1. A negligently fails to clean petroleum residue out of his
oil barge moored at a dock, thus creating the risk of harm to others
in the vicinity through fire or explosion of gasoline vapor. The
barge is struck by lightning and explodes, injuring B, a workman
on the dock. A is subject to liability to B. 2. A negligently leaves an obstruction in the public highway,
creating the risk that those using the highway will be injured by
collision with it. B's horse runs away with him and charges into
the obstruction, and b is injured. A is subject to liability to B. 3.

THE INTERVENTION OF A FORCE WHICH IS A NORMAL CONSEQUENCE OF A

TO PREVENT
§ 452. THIRD PERSON'S FAILURE TO
HARM. Failure of a third person to perform a duty
owing to another to protect him from harm threatened by the actor's negligent conduct is not a superseding cause of the other's harm. (1) EXCEPT AS STATED IN SUBSECTION (2), THE FAILURE OF A
THIRD PERSON TO ACT TO PREVENT HARM TO ANOTHER THREATENED BY THE
ACTOR'S NEGLIGENT CONDUCT IS NOT A SUPERSEDING CAUSE OF SUCH HARM. (2) WHERE, BY CONTRACT OR OTHERWISE, ALL RESPONSIBILITY FOR
THE PROTECTION OF THE OTHER AGAINST THE THREATENED HARM IS SHIFTED
TO THE THIRD PERSON, HIS INTENTIONAL OR NEGLIGENT FAILURE TO ACT
TO PREVENT SUCH HARM IS A SUPERSEDING CAUSE. Note to Institute: This Section has been changed by the addition
of Subsection (2). Neither the Advisers nor the Council have been able
to suggest better language. The Subsection appears necessary to cover a group of cases, in
substantial number, in which the failure of a third person to act has
been held to relieve the original actor of liability. The old analysis
of these cases was in terms of "termination of the risk."
This appears
to be clearly the wrong approach. The risk is not terminated. The
danger created by the actor is still alive, and the plaintiff is in
fact injured by that danger.

the third person, the relation between the third person and the plaintiff, the customs of the community in various types of situations, and
no doubt many others. Apparently the best that can be done is to make
a general statement as in Subs ection (2), and rely upon Comments and
Illustrations to indicate what is meant. The following cases indicate the problem:

§ 452
Torts

Comment:
a. The situation covered by both parts of this Section is that
in which, after the original actor has been negligent, and so has created an unreasonable risk of harm to another, a third person has the
opportunity, by taking affirmative action, to avert the threatened
harm. This implies that if such action were taken, it would prevent
the negligence of the original actor from causing the harm which has
in fact resulted. Comment on Subsection (1):
b. Subsection (1) states the rule applicable in the ordinary case,
that the failure of the third person to act to prevent harm to the other,
threatened by the original actor's negligent conduct, is not a superseding cause of such harm, and so does not relieve the actor of liability
for the harm which he has in fact caused. If the third person is under
a duty to the other to take such action, his failure to do so will subject him to liability for his own negligence, which is concurrent with
that of the actor, for the resulting harm which he has failed to prevent; but his failure to perform his duty does not relieve the original
actor of liability for the results of his own negligence.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
A fortiori,
where the third person is under no duty to the other to take any action,
but merely has the opportunity to do so, his failure to act not only
does not make him liable, but is not a superseding cause which will
relieve the original actor of liability. As to the exceptional cases
in which all responsibility has been shifted to the third person, see
Comments on Subsection (2). C. The rule stated in Subsection (1) applies not only where the
third person makes no effort to act to avert the harm, but also where
he makes such an affort, but the action which he takes is insufficient,
or is otherwise unsuccessful, in averting the harm. Illustrations:
1. A, the owner of a house abutting on a street in B City,
employs C to dig a trench across the highway to make a connection
with a sewer. C does the work of replacing the sidewalk so negligently that it is left in a condition dangerous for travel. A
knows of this, and B City is notified, but neither takes any
steps to put the sidewalk in safe condition. Several weeks after
C has completed the work D, walking on the sidewalk at night, and
without any negligence of his own, is hurt by a fall resulting
from the bad condition of the sidewalk. The failure of A, and
of B City, to have the sidewalk repaired, make both subject to
liability to D, but are not superseding causes relieving C of
liability to D.

An automobile negligently driven by A strikes B, and leaves
him on the highwaym unconscious and slowly bleeding to death. C,
a passing motorist, stops, looks over the situation, and decides to
drive on without doing anything to aid B. B bleeds to death. Regardless of whether C is under any duty to B to render such aid,
his failure to do so is not a superseding cause which will relieve
A of liability for the death of B. Comment on Subsection (2):
d. Subsection (2) covers the exceptional cases in which, because
the entire responsibility for the situation has been shifted to a third
person, the original actor is relieved of liability for the result which
follows from the operation of his own negligence. The shifted responsibility means in effect that the duty of obligation of the original actor
in the matter has terminated, and has been replaced by that of the third
person. e. One way in which the responsibility may be shifted is by contract between the actor and the third person. By express agreement, or
by fair implication from what is agreed, it may be understood that the
third person has taken over full responsibility for the situation, and
that the actor is relieved of his obligation. In many cases this is
not possible, since there are duties and obligations which cannot be
delegated or shifted to another.

Even in the absence of any contract or agreement, the circumstances may be such that the court will find that all responsibility
for the prevention of the harm has passed to the third person. It is
apparently impossible to state any comprehensive rule as to when such
a decision will be made. Various factors will enter into it. Among
them are the degree of danger and the magnitude of the risk of harm:
the character and position of the third person who is to take the responsibility, his knowledge of the danger, and the likelihood that he
will or will not exercise proper care, his relation to the plaintiff
or to the defendant, the lapse of time, and perhaps other considerations. The most that can be stated here is that when, by reason of
the interplay of such factors, the court finds that full responsibility
for control of the situation and prevention of the threatened harm has
passed to the third person, his failure to act is then a superseding
cause, which will relieve the original actor of liability. Illustrations:
1. The A Railroad negligently turns over to its connecting
carrier B Railroad a freight car, the door of which is in defective and dangerous condition. B Railroad operates the car on its
own line over a period of six months, during which time it negligently fails to inspect the car and discover the defect.

about near a schoolhouse. B, a boy, finds them and takes them
home. He plays with them for several weeks, during which time
C, his mother, discovers that he has the dynamite caps, knows
what they are, and fails to take them away from him. At the end
of that time B trades them to D, another boy, who is injured when

hood catch, creating the danger that on a rough highway the hood
will fly up and obscure the vision of the driver. The car is sold
by a dealer to B. A is notified of the defect in its car, and the
danger, and sends out to its dealers a new safety catch for installation in all such cars, in order to remedy the defect. The dealer
calls B, and offers him the new safety catch, urging him to install

The civil law, following its Roman predecessor,
took the position that all of these restrictions were
void. With the growth of English jurisprudence came
the cleavage in treatment of legacies and devises of
land previously referred to. This was most troublesome in the case of partial restraints upon marriage,
such as a gift to terminate if the recipient married
without consent. When the gift consisted of land, the
common law courts held the restraint valid. On the
other hand, the strict civil law rules required a finding of the invalidity of the restraint with respect to
legacies, considering a partial restraint as a mere
evasion of the rule forbidding general restraints.
The methods evolved by Chancery to escape from this
dilemma resulted in such formalistic rules as the "in
terrorem" doctrine. Under this doctrine, a partial
restraint upon marriage connected with a legacy was
held valid if a gift over upon breach was annexed.
Without the gift over, the restraint was regarded as
"in terrorem," that is, not intended to be operative
except insofar as it might induce performance by a
beneficiary who might not know it was void. This

of their gifts contingent upon divorce or separation,
violate public policy in that they make marriage
unstable. Such attempts are generally invalid under
the rule stated in §5.4.
It must be realized that to the extent a restraint
on marriage as a condition to obtaining or retaining
property is valid, it may encourage cohabitation
without marriage.
At the present time, this possibility has not undermined the validity of permissible
restraints on marriage.

statute. For example, there are statutes which make the owner of an
automobile liable as a defendant for any harm done to others by the

construed to impute the negligence of the driver to the owner to bar
his recovery for harm to the automobile.

negligence of a defendant with whom he is engaged in
a joint enterprise, the fact that they are so engaged
does not bar his recovery. a. Where negligence of a third person is imputed to the plaintiff under the rules stated in this Section, it bars his recovery
only to the extent that it would bar recovery if the negligence were
his own. The rules stated in §§ 467 to 484, and in particular the
rules as to the last clear chance stated in $$ 479 and 480, are applicable in determining whether the negligence is such a bar. b. Joint enterprise. A "joint enterprise" is in the nature of
a partnership, but is a broader and more inclusive term. In a partnership, there is a more or less permanent business arrangement, creating
a mutual agency between the partners for the purpose of carrying on
some general business dealings, so that the acts of one are to be
charged against the others. A jo int enterprise includes a partnership, but it also includes less formal arrangements for cooperation,
for a more limited period of time and a more limited purpose. It includes an undertaking to carry out a small number of activities or
objectives, or even a single one, entered into by members of the
group under such circumstances that all have a voice in directing
the conduct of the enterprise.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23

The law then considers that each is
the agent or servant of the others, and that the act of any one
within the scope of the enterprise is to be charged vicariously
against the rest. While it is by no means impossible that the
principle may be applied to other activities, the very great majority of the decisions applying it have involved the use of motor
vehicles. c. The elements which are essential to a joint enterprise are
commonly stated to be four: (1) an agreement, express or implied,
among the members of the group; (2) a common purpose to be carried
out by the group; (3) a community of pecuniary interest in that purpose, among the members; and (4) a right on the part of each member to
a voice in the direction of the enterprise, which gives him a share
in the right of control. Whether these elements exist is frequently
a question for the jury, under proper direction from the court. J. Partnership. A partnership is a joint enterprise and therefore each partner is responsible, not
only as defendant but also as plaintiff for the manner
in which his fellow partners conduct the partnership
activities. However, there are many joint enterprises
within the rule stated in this Section which are not
partnerships. d.

L Automobile trips. The question whether the
plaintiff is engaged in a joint enterprise with a negligent third person is usually important when two or
more persons are taking a ride or trip in an automobile or other vehicle and an accident happens through
the negligence of both the defendant and the driver of
the vehicle. When the plaintiff is a guest, as defined
in § 490, Comment a, the effect of the driver's negligence upon the plaintiff's right to recover is determined by the rule stated in that Section. Therefore, if
there is no prearrangement for a substantial sharing
of the expenses of the trip, as to which see Comment
the trip is not a joint enterprise merely because it is
made at the request of the plaintiff, because he and his
host have a common destination, because the destination or any change therein is to be determined by mutual agreement, because it is arranged that the guest
is to drive alternatively with his host, or even because
they are going to the common destination to accomplish a purpose in which they have a common but not
a business interest. No one of these facts, nor indeed
all of them together, is sufficient to justify a jury or
other trier of fact in finding that the trip was a joint
enterprise. J. Fellow servants in vehicle.

When the journey on which the plaintiff and
driver of the vehicle are participating is itself a part
of a business enterprise in which the parties are mutually interested, the two are engaged in a joint enterprise. It is immaterial that the particular journey is a
single transaction and is not a part of the general
course of a business in which they are associated as
partners or otherwise. It is also immaterial whether
the car is owned or hired by the one or the other or by
both jointly; the use of the car as a part of a common
business enterprise makes each responsible for the
manner in which it is operated both as defendant and
plaintiff. Thus, if two farmers by prior arrangement
or on a particular occasion use the car of one to transport their produce to market, the drive thereto is itself
a joint business enterprise, even though thereafter the
sale of the produce is the separate business of each. It
is, however, not enough that the journey is preparatory to the conduct of a business in which the two are
mutually interested. Thus, if the owner of the vehicle
and another are jointly interested in a business transaction to be carried on at a particular point, the fact
that the owner of the vehicle gives the other transportation to that point does not of itself make the journey
thereto a joint enterprise. Illustrations:
1.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
A and B are partners in a business carried
on in the City of X. They live in adjacent houses
in a suburb of X. The partners drive to town one
day in A's car, another day in B's car. In neither
case is the drive to their office in X a joint enterprise of A and B. 2. A, as attorney for B, is engaged in the trial of a case in the town of X. C is retained by B to
assist A. Both A and C live in the same village
which is at some distance from the town of X. On the day of the trial A offers to drive C to X. While on the way to X, A drives the car carelessly
and a collision ensues in which C is injured. A's
negligent driving does not bar C from recovering
against the driver of the negligently driven vehicle with which A's car collides.

The special
problems created by this interval are important, as
restraints upon marriage are most frequently employed
in testamentary dispositions. By specific language,
or under usual rules of construction, some testamentary limitations require the devisee or legatee to
remain single only during the interval prior to the

§ 491
Joint possession of vehicle. The fact that the
driver and another riding with him are in joint possession of the vehicle is sufficient to make any journey
taken by them therein a joint enterprise irrespective
of whether the journey is or is not made for a common
business purpose. This is so not only when the joint
possession arises from a joint hiring but also when it
pesults from a joint ownership. h. Joint possession of vehicle. The fact that the driver and
another who is riding with him are joint owners of the vehicle, or
in joint possession of it, as where they have rented it together,
may be sufficient to make the journey which they take in it a joint
enterprise. The common purpose, the common pecuniary interest, and
the right to an equal voice in the direction of the driving, can be
established by the relation into which they have entered. Neither
joint ownership nor joint possession, however, is necessarily enough
in itself to make any ride taken together in the vehicle a joint enterprise.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
Thus, even though a husband and wife are joint owners of
an automobile, or have rented it together, the understanding between
them may still be that the husband is to plan and conduct the journey, and drive the car without any right of inyerference from the
wife; that her position is that of a guest on the ride, and that any
suggestions she may make as to the driving are suggestions only, and
need not necessarily be followed, or heeded, on any basis of a mutual
right of direction or control. Such questions are frequently for the
jury, under proper direction from the court. g. Sharing expenses of trip. The fact that two g
more persons, who do not jointly hire or own the car,
agree that each shall pay a substantial share of the
expenses of a particular trip does not of itself make
the trip a joint enterprise. When, however, there are
one or more of the following additional factors the determination whether there is a joint enterprise is a
question for the jury subject to the power of the court
to see to it that the jury reaches reasonable conclusion. These factors are: (1) a common destination;
(2) a power to determine or change the route from
time to time by mutual agreement, and (3) the fact
that the trip is for a common but non-business purpose.

chunks.content:
For a limitation to constitute a restraint upon marriage it must have two characteristics.
First, there
must be an otherwise effective present disposition of
an interest in property, whether that interest be a
present or a future interest. Second, the acquisition
or retention of that interest must be dependent upon
the future conduct of the devisee or legatee which the
disposition is designed to influence. During the lifetime of the testator, there is not disposition of
property, but only the written manifestation of an
intention to make some future disposition to a particular devisee or legatee upon certain conditions.
Consequently, the provision is not within the rule
here stated even though, in fact, its existence in
the will prior to the death of the testator does
exert some coercion upon the prospective beneficiary
(see Comment a). At the death of the testator, the
will becomes a legally effective disposition of property.
If, by its terms, the devisee or legatee can benefit
only if then unmarried, no further conduct is thereby
The status if fixed; either the beneficiary
coerced.

1. Sharing expenses of trip. The fact that two or more persons,
who do not jointly own or hire the vehicle, agree that each shall pay
a substantial share of the expenses of a particular trip, is some evidence looking toward a joint enterprise. It is not, however, enough in
itself to establish that relation, since it is entirely consistent with
the position of one who is a mere guest in the automobile, who makes as
a courtesy to his host his own voluntary contribution toward the ride,
or, in the alternative, that of a paying passenger who has purchased
his transportation. In neither case does the person who so pays acquire any right to a voice, or to any measure of control, as to the
journey or the driving. In order that a joint enterprise may be found, there must be some
additional factors. If there is a common destination, a common purpose
in the journey, a common pecuniary interest in that purpose, and the
circumstances are such as to indicate a power to determine or change
the route or the manner of driving by majority vote or by mutual agreement, the joint enterprise may be found, and the sharing of expenses is
a factor of importance leading to the conclusion. It is, in other words,
a significant element taken together with others, but in itself is not
controlling. When plaintiff owns vehicle.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
The fact that the
plaintiff is the owner of the car which he permits another to drive does not make the journey during which
such other drives a joint enterprise, although his ownership may be important in three other particulars. First, it may give him a peculiar ability to control the
manner in which the driver operates the car, and
therefore, may bar his recovery against the negligent
defendant under the rule stated in § 495. An
owner of a car is entitled to expect that one whom he
permits to drive his car will follow his directions. On
the other hand, one who is a guest in a car not only
feels reluctant to interfere with his driver but the owner who is driving is far less likely to heed his advice

Comment on Subsection (2):
k. The rule stated in Subsection (1) bars the plaintiff from recovery against a third person who is not a member of the joint enterprise,
because of the negligence of another member of the enterprise. The
rules stated in Subsection (2) apply as between the members of the group
themselves. If the plaintiff is injured by the negligence of a defendant with whom he is engaged in a joint enterprise, his action against
that defendant is not barred by reason of the defendant's own negligence. As between two members of the joint enterprise, however, where neither
of them is himself negligent, neither can recover from the other for the
negligence of a third member of the enterprise. This is an application
of the agency rule, that where two principals both have the same agent,
his misconduct is to be charged against both of them in any action between them. Illustrations:

§ 493. BENEFICIARY UNDER A DEATH STATUTE. The effect of the contributing negligence of a
beneficiary under a death statute depends upon the
provisions of the statute. (1) THE NEGLIGENCE OF ONE BENEFICIARY UNDER A DEATH STATUTE DOES
NOT BAR RECOVERY FOR THE BENEFIT OF ANY OTHER BENEFICIARY. (2) WHETHER THE CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE OF A BENEFICIARY UNDER A
DEATH STATUTE BARS OR REDUCES RECOVERY TO THE EXTENT OF HIS OWN BENEFIT
DEPENDS UPON THE STA TU TE. [Note to Institute:
The Advisers and the Council agree that Sub-
There is very little left of the rule

others. The leading case in support of it, Hazel v. Hoopeston-Danville
Motor Bus Co., 1923, 310 Ill. 38, 141 N.E. 392, has recently been overruled in Nudd v. Matsoukas, Ill. 1956, 131 N.E. 2d 325.]
Comment:
a. Different types of death statutes. A "death
statute" is a statute which gives a right of action
against one who has wrongfully killed another. Any
person entitled to share in the amount recovered under
a death statute is a beneficiary thereunder. The right
to maintain such action is sometimes given to the executor or administrator of the victim, sometimes to his
next of kin. Death statutes vary in form and purpose.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23

The purpose of the more usual form of statute is to
compensate the survivors for the benefits which they
would have derived from the earning power of the decedent had his life not been cut short. The sum recovered is distributed in various ways by the various statutes among the survivors who, had the decedent lived,
would have benefited by his earning power. Where the
statute is of this type, the fact that a beneficiary is
himself guilty of negligence which contributed to the
death of the decedent does not prevent recovery unless
he is the sole beneficiary. It doce, however, affect the
amount recoverable. If one of the beneficiaries is
guilty of contributory negligence he is not allowed to
benefit by the statute. The amount which he would
have received had he not been negligent is deducted. from the amount recoverable by the survivors as a

THE NEGLIGENCE OF ONE PARENT DOES NOT BAR RECOVERY BY THE OTHER
PARENT FOR LOSS OF THE SERVICES OF THEIR CHILD. [Note to Institute: The Advisers have suggested that this Section
be added, and the Council have given it hesitant approval. There are
very few cases. In accord with the Section are Atlanta & C.A.L. R. Co. v. Gravitt, 1894, 93 Ga. 369, 20 S.E. 550; Illingworth v. Madden, 1937,
135 Me. 159, 192 A. 273; Macdonald v. O'Reilly, 1904, 45 Ore. 589, 78 P. 753. To the contrary is Beasley v. United States, D. S.C. 1948, 81 F. Supp. 518. Also Klepper v. Breslin, Fla. 1955, 83 So. 2d 587. In Crane v. Smith, 1944, 23 Cal. 2d 288, 144 P. 2d 356, and Keena
v. United Railroads of San Francisco, 1922, 57 Cal. App. 124, 207 P. 35,
the negligence was imputed because the damages recovered would be community property. This is meagre authority. The argument in favor of the Section is,
first, that $ 487 removes the imputation of contributory negligence from
one spouse to the other, as to other personal injury actions; second,
that § 493 removes it as to wrongful death actions. There is no reason
to make an exception as to loss of services.]
Comment:
a. Under the rule stated in § 487, the negligence of husband or
wife is not imputed to the other spouse to bar recovery for his or her
own physical harm.

the services of their child. b. As in the case of physical harm to one spouse, the rule sta ted
in this Section may be affected by the law of community property in a
small number of jurisdictions. See § 487, Comment c. It is also possible that negligence may be imputed upon some other basis than that of the
relation of parents, as for example where the parties are engaged in a
joint enterprise, under § 491, or where one is employed by the other,

$ 893. VOLUNTARY EXPOSURE TO RISK AS A DEFENSE
A PERSON WHO KNOWS THAT ANOTHER HAS CREATED A DANGER OR IS DOING A

Notes (§ 893)
Torts
72
Memorandum of Mr. Laurence H. Eldredge
to
The Council of the American Law Institute
Re: Restatement of Torts 2nd
Chapter 17A, Assumption of Risk
I object to the Reporter's statement of the topic "Assumption of Risk"
because I believe that it is fundamentally unsound analysis. In Section
496A he states as a general principle that "a plaintiff who voluntarily
assumes a risk of harm arising from the negligent or reckless conduct of
the defendant is not entitled to recover for such harm."
Under the Reporter's analysis, a defendant who is a tortfeasor can
none the less escape liability by what the Reporter calls "voluntary
assumption of risk." Upon any accurate analysis he is talking about one
particular type of contributory negligence, and this was clearly recognized by Professor Bohlen when he wrote Comment d to Section 466 of the
Restatement of Torts. The Reporter defends his analysis of voluntary assumption of risk by
saying that some of the courts have called certain types of contributory
negligence voluntary assumption of risk, and he is following what the
courts have done. It is true that the cases are in a confused state and
frequently the courts have failed to analyze the tort problem accurately. To me this is all the more reason for the American Law Institute to present an accurate analysis and thereby assist in dispelling the confusion.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
During the 27 years last past in which I have assisted in Restatement
work, I have always understood that one of the primary purposes of the
Restatements is to present an accurate analysis of the substantive law. We have not hesitated to coin words and use terminology completely unfamiliar to the courts in order to accomplish this important objective. The chapters of the Restatement of Torts which deal with the law of negligence and with legal cause have been repeatedly praised. In those
chapters we talk in very different terms from the language of the cases. The analysis of "utility of the conduct," "magnitude of the risk," and
the "hazard problem" did not reflect the language found in the cases. We
coined the terms "legal cause" and "superseding cause."
This, and much
more, was done for the purpose of accuracy of analysis as to the substantive law and clarity of statement. It achieved this purpose, and I believe
no part of the Restatement of Torts has been more valuable to the courts. In Comment b to Section 496A the Reporter correctly states, "'Assumption of risk' is a term which has been surrounded by much confusion, because
it has been used by the courts in at least four different senses and the
distinctions seldom have been made clear." This is a strong reason for the

Institute to make the distinctions clear and to limit the term "voluntary
assumption of risk" to its proper place in substantive tort law. There
is no need for any new terminology. It is just a question of using the
familiar terms "voluntary assumption of risk" and "contributory negligence," and making clear the important distinctions between them. I turn now to analyze the problem of "voluntary assumption of risk."
There are very few general principles in tort law, but there are a great
many different rules. One of the fundamental principles of tort law is
that a defendant who has harmed the plaintiff's body or his property with
the plaintiff's consent is not a tortfeasor at all. The surgeon who cuts
off my leg with my consent is not a tortfeasor. Neither is the man who
runs over me with his automobile after I have lain down on the road and
asked him to do so. This is based upon the individualistic concept that
so far as tort law (as distinct from criminal law) is concerned, a person
is free to do as he pleases with his own body. Volenti non fit injuria. In the true consent situation, "Barkis is willin'" to have his bodily
integrity invaded. The rule of voluntary assumption of risk is a variant
of this principle of consent.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
In the voluntary assumption of risk case,
Barkis may not be willing to suffer an invasion of bodily integrity, but
"Barkis is willin' " to assume the risk of such an invasion taking place. The defendant who invades the plaintiff's bodily integrity where there is
true voluntary assumption of risk is not a tortfeasor, just as the surgeon
who cuts off a leg with the patient's consent is not a tortfeasor. Such
a person cannot be referred to as being negligent because that word connotes a breach of duty, and in both consent cases and true voluntary assumption of risk cases the defendant has not breached any duty to the
plaintiff. He is not a wrongdoer. The plaintiff has not suffered legal
injury. That is clear from the Latin phrase which is the origin of voluntary
assumption of risk: Volenti non fit injuria. Judge Cardozo saw the problem clearly and stated it accurately in Murphy v. Steeplechase Amusement
Park, (1929) 250 N.Y. 479, 166 N.E. 173. A classic statement is that of
Lord Justice Bowen in Thomas v. Quartermaine, (1887) L.R. 18 Q.R.D. 685:
"The duty of an occupier of premises which have an element of danger upon
them reaches its vanishing point in the case of those who are cognizant of
the full extent of the danger, and voluntarily run the risk.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
Volenti non
fit injuria."
I believe that once it is conceded that the defendant has acted negligently with respect to the plaintiff (i.e., that he is a tortfeasor with
respect to the plaintiff), then the sole defense is contributory negligence;
and there is no place whatever for bringing in any doctrine of voluntary
assumption of risk as a defense. It is important to keep in mind that the
defendant may not be a tortfeasor with respect to the plaintiff because of
the plaintiff's state of mind (i.e., his voluntary assumption of the risk),
and yet the defendant's same act may make him a tortfessor and negligent
with respect to other persons. For example, take the illustration of a
plaintiff who receives a phone call informing him that his house a quarter

in a third-floor room. He rushes out to the highway and sees a very
drunk man about to drive down the road in an automobile and realizes his
condition. At the plaintiff's solicitation the drunk agrees to accept
plaintiff as a passenger. In operating his car incompetently the drunk
is not a tortfeasor to the plaintiff who has voluntarily assumed the risk,
and the drunk is not subject to liability to the plaintiff when the car
is wrecked and the plaintiff is injured. The drunk would be operating
the car negligently with respect to other persons on the highway. If a court fails to analyze this problem accurately and decides that
the defendant is negligent with respect to the plaintiff, i.e., that he
has breached a duty to the plaintiff himself, the court may well decide
that the issue of any affirmative defense must be passed upon by the jury. So far as the defense of contributory negligence is concerned, the plaintiff may reasonably have assumed the risk in view of the great necessity
of his getting home quickly. However, once it is clearly seen that the
defense of voluntary assumption of risk negates any vilation of duty by
the defendant to the plaintiff, we are no longer concerned with determining what the reasonable man would do in the circumstances.

There would

as to just what the facts were, in which event the jury would have to perform its function as fact-finder. This would be done under proper instructions from the court that if they found the plaintiff has voluntarily assumed the risk they must find for the defendant even though the plaintiff
acted reasonably under the circumstances. I believe that our rules concerning voluntary assumption of risk
should be confined to analyzing the types of situations in which the
plaintiff's state of mind precludes the existence of a tort at all. Everything else should be included in the chapter on contributory negligence. There are two types of contributory negligence. In the first
type plaintiff inadvertently encounters a danger. This may result from
his careless inattention to his surroundings or his failure to appreciate
the risk which a reasonable man would appreciate. The second type of
contributory negligence is where the plaintiff presses on in the face of
a known danger and the magnitude of the risk to him outweighs the utility
of his conduct.

negligently to the plaintiff, i.e., he is a tortfeasor with respect to
the plaintiff. This is made clear in clauses (a) and (b) of Section 466
and the comment thereto. However, the present Comment e to that Section
does not correctly distinguish the two different things which I have emphasized. The Reporter has been somewhat concerned with certain procedural
problems which may arise in a trial with respect to the separate defenses
of contributory negligence and voluntary assumption of risk. We should
not be concerned with them. It is our job to make an accurate statement

The confusion which is created in even a brilliant analytical mind by

Little express justification exists for the technical
condition-limitation distinction. The sole policy
reason articulated in the decisions espousing this
distinction is the negative effect of interference
with the substantial interest of a third party which
could occur if a restraint within a limitation was
declared invalid. See items 3 and 6 below.
3.
Historical Note
——
The historical origin
of restraints on first marriages provides some
rationale for the condition-limitation distinction.
Although the English courts adopted their general
rule against restraints from the Romans, who allowed
absolutely no restraints on first marriages, several
exceptions to the general prohibition were created
by the English judges. This was a time when parental
involvement in marriage was looked upon with approval
by the citizenry, and courts were eager to find
exceptions to the general rule against restraints.
These English authorities were the first to state
that the special limitation was not subject to the
same policy considerations as the condition subsequent.

Torts
76
Memorandum of Professor Wex S. Malone
I agree with a great deal that Larry Eldredge has had to say in his
memorandum. I fear, however, that I find myself out of accord with him in
one very important respect. I therefore offer the following outline of
the matter, as I see it. Assumption of Risk situations appear to me to fall into three categories. First, are those situations where there is an advance express acceptance of risk, as indicated in Prosser's Section 496 (b). Secondly,
there are those situations where the plaintiff's knowledge of danger, and
his procedure in the face of it amount to conduct that is unreasonable,
and hence should be regarded as contributory negligence. Up to this point,
I feel that we are all in accord. Third (and here I find myself out of accord with Larry) are those
situations where the defendant's duty can be fully discharged by affording
a warning. This would be true in the case of seen trespassers, licensees,
and was probably unqualifiedly true of business guests or invitees at one
time. Also to be included here are the duties to social guests in vehicles
who are injured because of the defective condition of the vehicle or the
incompetence of the driver.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
In those cases the limited character of the
defendant's duty, it seems to me, is the underlying reason why the plaintiff who knowingly encounters the dangerous condition cannot recover. For
if the defendant can discharge the full measure of his responsibility by
affording knowledge of the danger to the plaintiff, it follows that where
the plaintiff is possessed of such knowledge independently of any warning
that might be required, the failure to give the warning plays no causal
part in bringing about the injury. I understand from Larry's memo that in all instances where the plaintiff has knowledge of the danger (irrespective of the nature of the defendant's duty) there can be no recovery. To my mind this is equivalent to a
statement that a defendant can always discharge his duty by giving a warning. This, I submit, is entirely too broad. Even in Thomas v. Quartermaine, on which Larry relies (and which I
would hope does not support the modern state of affairs), Bowen made it
clear that a duty to warn was all that was owed under the circumstances
of the case. He said:
"His duty was not to make the premises safe, but to make it as
safe as it looked--to remove a hidden danger or make it known. 11
It also seems to me that Bohlen makes abundantly clear the same proposition with respect to the Assumption of Risk by an employee.

that the plaintiff has knowledge of the danger is important only because
the only duty of the defendant was to see to it that the plaintiff was not
exposed to hidden danger. [Bohlen, Voluntary Assumption of Risk, (1910) 20
Harvard Law Review 14, 911. It follows as a natural corollary that if the

Torts
78
Reply by the Reporter
The position of the Confederate Army, as the Reporter understands it,
is that there is no such defense as "implied" assumption of risk; and that
what passes by that name is always either a matter of no duty on the part of
the defendant, or of contributory negligence on the part of the plaintiff. The Reporter finds this little short of astounding. It is in flat
contradiction of the position taken by the first Restatement in § 893 (see
Note at the start of this Chapter). It throws into the ashcan the language,
and the stated basis of the holdings, of literally thousands of cases; and
so far as the Reporter is aware it is supported, if at all, only by a bare
three or four sporadic cases, all explainable on other grounds. There are
many decisions, of course, which have said, in particular situations, that
assumption of risk overlaps contributory negligence; and it may certainly
be arguable that where this is true, the defense should be governed by the
same rules as contributory negligence; but it is another thing entirely to
say that there is no such defense. The position is all the more surprising since, as the Reporter understands it, it is conceded that express assumption of risk is valid, and
that it is a defense, and that § 496B below is a correct statement of that
rule.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
In other words, if the plaintiff accepts the risk by words, it is
assumption of risk, and matter of defense. But he cannot do tacitly and
by conduct what he can do by words; and when it is claimed that he does,
there is no such defense, and it is always a question either of duty or of
contributory negligence. It is submitted that this, in the face of so many
cases, makes no great amount of sense. The following distinctions may be pointed out, between assumption of
risk and duty on the one hand, and assumption of risk and contributory
negligence on the other. Assumption of Risk and Duty
Part of the confusion under which the Confederates labor is due to
the fact that certain defendants, and particular possessors of land, are
under only a limited duty to particular plaintiffs. Typical is the duty
of a possessor toward a licensee, which, as to conditions of the land, is
only to disclose latent conditions of which he knows and the licensee does
not. For historical reasons, the law developed here as a matter of duty,
with the burden upon the plaintiff to prove that he was unaware of the
condition, that the defendant knew of it, and that he did not disclose it. The initial cases were decided before the defense of assumption of risk
was recognized at all. But most negligence duties are not limited in this manner.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23

The duty,
if it exists at all, is ordinarily a full duty of reasonable care. Disclosure, or warning, as Professor Malone has pointed out, may or may not
be enough to satisfy the duty, depending upon all of the circumstances.

or unreasonably (facts can be assumed which make it either) continues

Undoubtedly assumption of risk and contributory negligence often
overlap, and in most cases of assumption of risk both defenses are
available, and it does not make the slightest difference which name is
given. The two are related to one another as intersecting circles, and
the area of intersection is a large one. This does not mean, however,
that they are always identical. As has been said many times, assumption of risk is a matter of the plaintiff's voluntary acceptance of
the risk--his consent, express or implied, to assume it; while contributory negligence is a matter of his failure to exercise reasonable
care to protect himself against it. Either may exist without the other. There are the following possible distinctions, which merit consideration:
1. Contributory negligence is always unreasonable conduct.

understand and appreciate it, whether a reasonable man would do so or not. (See $496D, and Mr. Eldredge's memorandum). There are a number of cases
which support this, and the Reporter, after thought, agrees that they are
right. This is notwithstanding certain other decisions which hold that
the plaintiff cannot be heard to say that he did not know of certain risks,
as, for example, that of falling, or of being burned by fire. What is clear, however, is that an objective standard is always
applied to contributory negligence. As in the case of negligence itself
(see $ 290), the individual is required to know what the standard reasonable man would know, and his ignorance of the risk will not prevent a
finding that he is negligent in encountering it. In this the two defenses obviously stand on a different footing. 11

the defendant is "wilful, "wanton," or "reckless." (See § 482). Assumption of risk is a defense in such cases.

The "Confederate Army"--so designated by the Reporter, I suppose, in
the expectation that theirs will be a Lost Cause--would agree with the Reporter that express consent is a valid defense to an action for negligence
--whether this defense is called consent, or assumption of risk, or volenti
non fit injuria. They would, I am sure, agree with him, too, that there
may be an implied consent and thus an implied assumption of risk. Their
difference with him is not that they deny that actual consent, or true
assumption of risk, may be indicated by conduct as well as express language, but that they insist that consent is a meaningful, intelligible
concept rather than a mere fiction, to be automatically applied when
there is knowledge of danger. Thus
The Reporter regards assumption of risk as based on consent. in § 496D, Comment b, he says, "The basis of assumption of risk is the
plaintiff's consent to accept the risk and look out for himself. And in
his last memorandum he says that "assumption of risk is a matter of what
the plaintiff in fact knows and is willing to accept." Yet he wants to
apply the concept whenever the plaintiff is fully aware of the nature of
the risk involved and still nevertheless proceeds with his course of conduct.

To say that the plaintiff necessarily "consents" under these circumstances is to give a completely different meaning to consent and to
make a fiction of it. There are two kinds of negligent conduct. The first is inadvertent,
with the actor proceeding without any recognition of or regard to the
risks involved. The second is more deliberate, with the actor having
awareness to a greater or lesser degree of the risks involved, but proceeding with his conduct just the same. When we are concerned with the
conduct of the defendant, we draw no particular distinction between the
two types of conduct (unless it is of such a character that it may be
characterized as wanton misconduct). In either case, we apply an objective standard and we speak of balancing the magnitude of the risk
against the utility of the risk. If a defendant exceeds the speed limit,
the test is the same whether he failed to look at the speedometer or knew
that he was going too fast. If he ran a red light, the test is the same
whether he failed to see the trafic light or saw that it was red. If a
light fixture fell from the ceiling in his store, the test is the same
whether he failed to discover the defective condition, or he discovered
it and decided that it would be all right to leave it alone for a week
longer until his electrician returned from a vacation.

apply to assumption of risk are normally illustrations of misunderstanding of the true nature of assumption of risk--a type of misunderstanding
which would became commonplace if the Reporter's recommendations are
adopted. I have limited my memorandum to the situation where it is determined
that the defendant has breached his duty to the plaintiff to use care-where the defendant is negligent. It is here, I think, that most harm
has been done by the careless--I almost said, negligent--use of the term,
assumption of risk. Setting true consent (express or implied) aside, it
is wrong to say that a negligent defendant can have two defenses--contributory negligence and assumption of risk--or that a plaintiff whose conduct was reasonable can still not recover because of a finding that he
assumed the risk.

defendant. Messrs. Eldredge and Malone have covered this adequately. I
agree with them that it would be much better not to speak of assumption

is inaccurate and somewhat misleading I do not have the feeling that a
great amount of harm has been done by it. Perhaps a reasonable compromise could be reached between the Reporter and the Confederates by a
section on this matter, indicating that accurate analysis treats this
as a duty question, but that it is frequently handled as an affirmative
defense. As I recall the vote at Buck Hill Falls, Professor James and I
took an intermediate position to this effect on the ground that it would
accord proper weight both to accurate analysis and to the state of the
authorities.

Memorandum of Professor Warren A. Seavey
I am not going to write an extensive memorandum on assumption

However, I would be glad if, when you are presenting your point of view,
you would mention that I believe that assumption of risk is a negative
rather than an affirmative defense, and that it represents only situations in which the defendant has violated no duty to the plaintiff. One
who accepts a ride with a drunken driver assumes as to the driver the

the risks which he is taking, does not assume a risk, since an approaching
motorist still owes him a duty of care. I think these illustrations point
out my view.
Hoping that the truth will prevail,
Warren A. Seavey

§ 496A
Torts

$496A. GENERAL PRINCIPLE
A PLAINTIFF WHO VOLUNTARILY ASSUMES A RISK OF HARM ARISING FROM THE
NEGLIGENT OR RECKLESS CONDUCT OF THE DEFENDANT CAN NOT RECOVER FOR SUCH
HARM. Comment:
a. This Section states the general principle of assumption of risk. As to the application of the principle to particular situations, see the
following Sections 496B to 496G. b. The defense whose general principle is stated in this Section is
given the name, in most jurisdictions, of "assumption of risk." A few
courts have limited the use of that term to cases of master and servant,
or in some instances to other relations where there is a contract between
the parties. Such courts have applied the same principle to other situations under the ancient maxim, "Volenti non fit injuria," which signifies
that no wrong is done to one who consents. The distinction is, however,
one without a difference, of terminology only, and the rules applied are
the same in either case. c. Meanings of assumption of risk. "Assumption of risk" is a term
which has been surrounded by much confusion, because it has been used by
the courts in at least four different senses, and the distinctions seldom
have been made clear. These meanings are as follows:
1.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:
In its simplest form, assumption of risk means that the plaintiff
has given his express consent to relieve the defendant of an obligation to
exercise care for his protection, and agrees to take his chances as to
injury from a known or contemplated risk. The result is that the defendant, who would otherwise be under a duty to exercise such care, is relieved
of that responsibility, and is no longer under any duty to protect the
plaintiff. As to such express assumption of risk, see § 496B. 2. A second, and closely related meaning, is that the plaintiff has
entered voluntarily into some relation with the defendant which he knows
to involve the risk, and so is regarded as tacitly or impliedly agreeing
to relieve the defendant of responsibility, and to take his own chances. Thus a spectator entering a baseball park may be regarded as consenting
that the players may proceed with the game without taking precautions to
protect him from being hit by the ball. Again the legal result is that
the defendant is relieved of any duty to the plaintiff. As to such implied assumption of risk, see § 4960. 3. In a third type of situation the plaintiff, aware of a risk created by the negligence of the defendant, proceeds or continues voluntarily
to encounter it.

chunks.source: Restatement of the law, second, torts. Submitted by the council. Tentative draft[s] no. 1-23
chunks.content:

has been furnished by his employer with a machine which is in dangerous
condition, and that the employer, after notice, has failed to repair it
